title: In the Wake of the 2024 Floods in Southern Brazil: Restore the Past or Rethink the Future?
text:
In the Wake of the 2024 Floods in Southern Brazil: Restore the Past or Rethink the Future?

In May 2024, the floods that hit Rio Grande do Sul exposed a contradiction common to contemporary cities. Many were built alongside rivers and shaped by their presence, yet spent decades trying to control water without incorporating its dynamics into urban planning. Extreme weather events will intensify that vulnerability. More than two years later, reconstruction in the Brazilian state has progressed, infrastructure has been restored, and new protection strategies are taking shape. But are these cities rebuilding their relationship with water, or only restoring the systems that failed?

title: "Nothing Starts From Zero": In Conversation With Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa of FADAA
text:
"Nothing Starts From Zero": In Conversation With Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa of FADAA

Following a seven-year pause, Amman Design Week returned in 2026 under the theme "Accumulations," bringing together designers, makers, and cultural practitioners to reflect on the work shaping Jordan's design landscape. The fourth edition, held from October 2 to 17, 2026, marked a new chapter for the event, with architects Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa, founders of the architecture and design practice FADAA, serving as co-directors. Their appointment also brought their research-driven approach to the event's broader program, which explored the relationships between daily practices, cultural memories, and material environments. During the event, we had the opportunity to speak with Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa about the thinking behind this year's theme, their approach to material investigations, and how practicing in Jordan informs their work across architecture, objects, and public space.

title: How Surface Materials Shape Contemporary Interiors
text:
How Surface Materials Shape Contemporary Interiors

Whether in residential interiors, workplaces, hospitality environments, or public spaces, the relationship between aesthetic intentions and technical performance can redefine how surfaces are used and how they perform. A material selected for its specific color, texture, or finish must remain visually coherent when applied to furniture fronts, cabinetry, countertops, and other interior elements. Yet how can architects and designers create visually distinctive and tactilely engaging interiors while preserving their original design intentions across different applications?

title: Herzog & de Meuron and EHDD to Transform a Mid-Century Warehouse into the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity
text:
Herzog & de Meuron and EHDD to Transform a Mid-Century Warehouse into the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity

The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity has unveiled the masterplan for its forthcoming archives in Marin County, California. The project, designed by Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron and Bay Area-based EHDD, transforms a mid-century modern warehouse into a cultural destination, with art installation space, flexible galleries, learning and gathering spaces, a theater, and dining offerings. The large-scale adaptive reuse project is accompanied by a transformation of the gardens and grounds of the surrounding 88.5-acre site, led by Field Operations. While the Institute's Eames Archives will form one part of the museum, its exhibitions and programming are intended to extend far beyond the work of Charles and Ray Eames, bringing together different disciplines, creative processes, and ideas.

title: Lion Green Road / Mary Duggan Architects
text:
Lion Green Road / Mary Duggan Architects

Lion Green Road is a residential-led scheme comprising five buildings containing 157 dwellings. The project sits within a verdant landscape in Coulsdon, London Borough of Croydon, within a geographical chalk basin. The wider context is varied typologically, including an extensive low-rise green belt development to the south on higher ground by Barratt Homes, delivering 667 homes alongside retained extensive lush open land. A traditional low-rise suburban grain populates the northern side of the site, also ascending toward Crystal Palace.

title: Foster + Partners and MANICA Unveil Design for New Stadium to Replace Milan's San Siro
text:
Foster + Partners and MANICA Unveil Design for New Stadium to Replace Milan's San Siro

AC Milan and FC Internazionale Milano (Inter) have unveiled the design for Generali Stadium, a 71,500-seat venue planned to become the shared home of the two football clubs in Milan, Italy. Designed by Foster + Partners and MANICA, the new stadium will be built alongside the existing San Siro as part of a 281,000-square-meter redevelopment of the surrounding area. The project follows years of discussions over the future of the historic venue, which the clubs acquired in 2025 with the intention of replacing it. Construction is expected to begin in 2028, with the stadium scheduled to host its first match during the 2031/32 season, subject to planning approvals.

title: When the Outdoors Becomes Home: A New Generation of Outdoor Kitchens
text:
When the Outdoors Becomes Home: A New Generation of Outdoor Kitchens

Outdoor kitchens are no longer just an exclusive accessory; they have become a natural extension of the home. Gardens, terraces, and porches are transforming into spaces where cooking and, above all, entertaining can take place without having to step inside. In addition to offering convenience, this solution increases property value and responds to a lifestyle that is increasingly connected to the outdoors.

title: Minimalist House / FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects
text:
Minimalist House / FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects

Situated on a hill rising from the lakeside town, this residence was planned for a single owner. The home was designed to incorporate the lake view as part of daily life. When hearing "a home for a single occupant", people typically imagine a compact house. Yet, living alone is not simply about having fewer residents. Without the need for family-oriented layouts or shared spaces, the house can be conceived with the individual as the base unit, starting from physical perception and rhythm of life.

title: SE House / Kantor Gunawan Gunawan
text:
SE House / Kantor Gunawan Gunawan

SE House stands as a quiet manifesto for tropical living, conceived as an urban oasis that reinterprets Australian-inspired design for Surabaya's vibrant context. Anchored by a courtyard that reflects the owner's attentiveness to landscape, the residence embodies natural sensibilities through design choices that promote airflow, permeability, and daily connection to foliage inside and out. Its philosophy is subtle yet deliberate, expressed through materiality and spatial choreography rather than overt displays of greenery.

title: House in Yakami / enter-archi
text:
House in Yakami / enter-archi

House in Yakami explores how architecture can respond to the landscape through bodily experience, rather than simply consuming its beauty as a view. The site is located in Yakami, Onan Town, Shimane Prefecture, surrounded by the Chugoku Mountains.

title: The House of Courtyards / Studio VDGA
text:
The House of Courtyards / Studio VDGA

Set in the city of gold, Dubai, this villa was one of the most challenging projects considering the diverse architectural languages that the city follows. Be it the towering skyscrapers, extremely modern boxed structures, or ornate villas, the city sees a lot in spatial expression. Various themes were scrapped, and many ideas were renegotiated till we found a form that very closely mirrors desert architecture.

title: Escola Sant Ignasi-Jesuïtes de Sarrià / Aquidos
text:
Escola Sant Ignasi-Jesuïtes de Sarrià / Aquidos

Sant Ignasi School, inaugurated in 1892 and designed by architect Joan Martorell, is an emblematic building in Barcelona that has welcomed thousands of students since its foundation. Its architectural composition is characterized by symmetry, organized around a central axis defined by the garden and pond.

title: U-shaped store / MANERA
text:
U-shaped store / MANERA

U-shaped Store is a children's store designed by MANERA atelier. The project explores the relationship between retail space, scenography, and architecture, proposing a flexible environment organized around a central void.

title: Beyond Affordable Housing: Integrating Civic Infrastructure in US Mixed-Use Developments
text:
Beyond Affordable Housing: Integrating Civic Infrastructure in US Mixed-Use Developments

For much of the twentieth century, affordable housing in the United States was conceived as a distinct residential category, shaped by financing structures and development practices that separated housing for lower-income residents from the broader civic and commercial functions of the city. Federal housing legislation and subsequent urban renewal policies contributed to the construction of large residential developments that were frequently financed and managed independently of surrounding urban infrastructure. The consequences of this approach, including concentrated poverty, deteriorating buildings, unequal access to services, and the eventual demolition of prominent public housing projects, are extensively documented.

title: KOI Restaurant / SOA Architekti
text:
KOI Restaurant / SOA Architekti

The restaurant in Košice occupies a corner building in the historic city centre, in a space that previously housed a clothing or furniture store. The business is run by a father and son. The father brings personal experience, a strong sense of family tradition, and an openness to blending diverse culinary influences into the concept. The son contributes a contemporary gastronomic approach, an understanding of a younger audience, and the energy of an urban venue designed not only for dining but for all-day social life.

title: Konya Square Houses and Bicycle Museum Extension / Yalin Architectural Design
text:
Konya Square Houses and Bicycle Museum Extension / Yalin Architectural Design

Konya Square Houses consists of 13 reinforced-concrete buildings constructed in 2005, drawing on the traditional Konya houses and neighborhood fabric that existed on the site until 1955. Over the years, the complex accommodated various non-governmental organizations and municipal departments.

title: DamDam House / Studio SMA + Ground Architects
text:
DamDam House / Studio SMA + Ground Architects

DamDam is a compact house for a couple, their twins, and two cats, designed with solid exterior walls to ensure privacy on a small site surrounded by taller buildings. Working within the constraints of the parking layout, the functions of each floor were carefully separated, and the circulation was precisely planned to maximize the usability of the interior spaces.

title: Virtual Studio at the Cidade das TIC, A Coruña Arms Factory / Diaz y Diaz Architects
text:
Virtual Studio at the Cidade das TIC, A Coruña Arms Factory / Diaz y Diaz Architects

In the former Weapons Factory of A Coruña, the Virtual Studio translates an essential duality into architecture: a hermetic box designed to create digital worlds versus an open volume that dialogues with the landscape and the industrial memory of the site.

title: Alaska Airlines Flagship Lounge / Graham Baba Architects
text:
Alaska Airlines Flagship Lounge / Graham Baba Architects

At the Alaska Airlines Flagship Lounge in SeaTac International Airport, the door is always open. Travelers seek lounges as an escape from the anxiety, noise, and commotion of the concourse. Traditionally, airport lounges catered to this desire by emphasizing exclusivity: sleek, business-oriented safe havens that prioritized the needs of a privileged swath of travelers. Alaska Airlines sought to transform the lounge typology by providing a warm, welcoming space where all guests could find refuge – to relax, work, refuel and connect – a home-away-from-home with a sense of place deeply rooted in the Pacific Northwest. Programmatically, the lounge is conceived in four zones: Come In, an approachable entry; Help Yourself, a casual bistro; Take a Breath, a haven for peaceful relaxation; and Cut Loose, a cozy bar atmosphere. Lightly separated with an array of oak and twisted metal screens, the spaces flow together.

title: Brooklin Apartment / Küster Brizola Arquitetos
text:
Brooklin Apartment / Küster Brizola Arquitetos

Designed by the firm Küster Brizola Arquitetos, this 200-square-meter apartment in Brooklin, São Paulo, turns the traditional checkerboard floor into the main protagonist of the project, developed for a couple with two children. The residence was born from the desire to create a home focused on gathering, hosting friends and family, and building cherished memories, reinterpreting the classic pattern as the organizing element of the social area and the apartment's identity.

title: How to design transparent AI cost controls
text:
How to design transparent AI cost controls

A practical guide to choosing usage units, designing spending limits, and explaining AI costs before, during, and after the work.

Every AI response has a price. People often discover it only when a limit hits or a bill arrives.

A quick edit and a long-running agent can look almost identical in the interface. One finishes in seconds. The other might read hundreds of files, call external tools, and retry steps along the way. Yet both start with the same button.

Meanwhile, AI products keep changing what they charge for: requests, credits, tasks, usage allowances. Showing more technical numbers won’t make those costs easier to understand. People want to know what a job might use, whether it’s worth running, and what they can do to spend less.

For designers, that comes down to two decisions:

  1. The unit: what users see themselves spending.
  2. The moment: when they understand the cost — before, during, or after the work.

Under the hood: what a token is

A token is a unit a model reads or generates. A tokenizer breaks text into pieces: words, parts of words, punctuation, sometimes even spaces. For English, a useful rough estimate is that one token represents about three-quarters of a word. So a million text tokens might represent around 750,000 English words. The exact count depends on the tokenizer, language, and content.

  • Input and output cost different amounts. Model providers commonly charge more for tokens they generate than tokens they read. On several current models, output is about five times the price of standard input. Longer answers, reasoning, and repeated attempts can change the economics of what looks like one request.
  • Model choice matters. Output-token prices can differ by tens of times — or more — across models. A request that is cheap in a lightweight model can cost considerably more in a frontier model. The user’s task hasn’t changed, but the meter has.
  • Modality changes the calculation. Text, images, audio, and video don’t share one universal token conversion. A short prompt, an image attachment, and a five-minute clip may all look like inputs to the same composer, yet require very different amounts of processing. Some providers charge by tokens, others by frames, seconds, or generation settings.

For a sense of scale, a 15-word prompt might be around 20 text tokens. A 1092 × 1092 image has been estimated at roughly 1,600 image tokens using one image-accounting method. For video, Google’s published static-processing examples imply roughly 30,000–90,000 tokens for five minutes, depending on the resolution setting. Those estimates come from different systems, so they cannot be priced as though they were the same kind of token. That limitation is part of the lesson: a single input box hides very different work.

Why showing tokens fails

Tokens are the system’s currency, not the user’s. People budget in money, time, attention, and finished work. They feel the effects of tokens through longer waits, changing quotas, and unexpected charges — not by counting them.

“382,000 tokens used” may be technically precise. It doesn’t tell someone whether the next research run will fit within their allowance, which part of the job was expensive, or what to change next time.

The job isn’t just to disclose a number. It’s to translate system cost into something people can make decisions with.

Predictability beats precision

There’s a useful parallel outside AI. In a study of 10,882 internet subscribers, Lambrecht and Skiera (2006) found that many customers chose a flat-rate plan even when a metered plan would have been cheaper. In one group, nearly half made that choice; more than half of them paid at least twice what they needed to.

The researchers described two reasons:

  • Insurance effect: paying more can feel worthwhile if it removes the risk of a variable bill.
  • Taxi meter effect: people enjoy a service less when they have to watch the meter climb.

The study was about internet tariffs, not AI, so it doesn’t prove how AI subscribers behave. But it captures a tension designers know well: people want to understand what they’re spending without being forced to calculate every interaction.

A good AI cost interface gives them that predictability without pretending the underlying costs are fixed.

Decision 1: choose the unit

Before designing a meter or a pricing screen, decide what people see themselves spending.

There isn’t one perfect unit. Raw tokens expose the model’s actual consumption, which is useful in API consoles but hard to reason about in a product workflow. Dollars are easier to recognize, especially for teams managing a budget, but the amount can still change from one run to the next.

Some products charge in natural units such as minutes of audio, pages processed, or GPU time. Others use credits: a product-specific currency that lets very different AI features draw from one balance. Credits simplify billing, but people have to learn what they’re worth.

Closer to the work itself are tasks and actions — one generation, enrichment, or run — and outcomes, where a charge depends on a defined result. These are easier to count because they resemble what the user asked for. They also shift more uncertainty to the vendor: a 200-page document and a one-page email might both count as one summary, despite costing very different amounts to process.

At the other end are usage allowances, where people work within a pool or reset window, and invisible usage, where a feature is included without showing a meter at all.

The important distinction is who carries the uncertainty. Tokens and metered dollars pass more of it to the user. Tasks and outcomes put more of it on the vendor. A usage allowance protects people from per-action calculations, but can leave them guessing when they’ll hit the limit.

Neither end works for everything. That’s why many products use a hybrid approach — an included allowance for everyday work, with separate limits or paid usage for expensive actions.

When to show a price — and when to hide it

A visible cost makes people more careful. That’s helpful for an expensive batch, but exhausting for everyday chat.

For discrete, potentially expensive work — enriching 500 rows, rendering a video, or scheduling a nightly automation — show the price or a credible range before the user commits. That number matters to the decision.

For frequent, exploratory actions like chatting, small edits, or code suggestions, a usage allowance is often better. Putting a price on every interaction turns experimentation into budgeting. But when one job is unusually expensive, even inside a subscription, make an exception: show its likely cost before it starts. The goal isn’t to hide spending; it’s to show it when someone can still act on it.

Usage limits

Instead of pricing each action, the product gives users a pool and shows how much remains. It’s familiar from subscriptions and easy to understand — until the pool disappears unexpectedly.

Where it fits: Consumer and prosumer plans with frequent, exploratory actions.
What good looks like: Users can tell what’s left, when it resets, and what will happen at the limit.
Why it works. Limits remove the need to do arithmetic every time someone sends a message. The user can focus on the work, with a fairly predictable subscription price.

  • Show each time window and its reset. Claude uses short session limits alongside weekly limits. A line such as “resets in 1 hr 36 min” beside “resets Friday at 8:00 AM” gives people a plan. “Resets soon” doesn’t.
  • Separate genuinely different pools. In the examples above, Cursor distinguishes model usage categories and Claude breaks out a top-model allowance. That helps users connect a decision — using a more expensive model — to the quota it affects. Don’t split pools simply because the billing system happens to have multiple internal counters.
  • Explain the overflow order. Show what is consumed first, what happens next, whether on-demand spending is enabled, and where an actual cap applies. Users shouldn’t need to infer the order from three settings screens.
  • Give temporary promotions an end date. Claude advertises a temporary higher allowance. Stating when standard limits return avoids making the end of a promotion feel like a stealth reduction.
  • Offer an alternative to upgrading. A saved or banked reset in Codex can restore eligible usage windows, subject to plan and expiry rules. Waiting for the reset, switching modes, or reducing scope can be just as important

Tasks and outcomes

Per-action units count something users already recognize: a generation, enrichment, run, or task. The appeal is that the decision and the charge use the same language.

Where it fits: Automations and actions that are easy to count.
What good looks like: Someone can estimate a month’s workload and get close to the bill.

Zapier is a useful reference. In the captured plan, the interface shows “Included tasks: 119 / 750” and “Additional tasks ($0.05/task): 0 / 1,500.” Users can distinguish the included pool from overflow, see the unit price, and understand the potential ceiling.

The more important detail is what Zapier doesn’t count. Triggers, filters, and certain built-in steps don’t count as tasks; successful action steps generally do, while errored steps don’t. Those rules answer a question that matters as much as the price: who pays for failure?

Why it works. An action is legible. If the same action consistently costs the same amount, users can forecast and compare.

Do: Explain what counts, what doesn’t, and how failed or repeated attempts are treated. Give overages their own unit price and ceiling.

Don’t: Call something an outcome if customers can’t independently tell whether it happened.

Credits

Credits let a product use one balance across different features: chat, app building, hosting, deployments, enrichment, or external services. They’re useful, but no one arrives with an intuition for what one credit is worth.

Where it fits: Products offering several expensive AI features under one account.
What good looks like: Users understand both the credit’s approximate value and why a particular action consumed it.

Why it works. Credits make unlike actions comparable and let providers adjust underlying costs without rebuilding the subscription. The left-hand screenshot shows several pools — daily, monthly, rollover, and top-ups — with different expiry rules. The right-hand example attributes deductions to projects and jobs and maintains a running balance. That’s useful accounting.

Where it breaks. The screenshots show several familiar problems:

  • No transferable sense of value. A 50-credit pack priced at $30 works out to $0.60 per credit. A different product’s 3,000-credit pack for $500 is about $0.17 per credit. The name is the same, but the unit isn’t. These are snapshot prices from the illustrations, not a shared market rate.
  • Fractional deductions without context. “Agent Call: −0.77” is precise but doesn’t tell users what the call achieved.
  • Unexplained differences. A deployment costs 50 credits and an agent call costs 0.77. A ledger can record that difference without helping anyone understand it.
  • Promotions mixed into accounting. A “20% More” top-up offer belongs in the purchasing flow. On a usage-history screen, it competes with the reason someone opened that screen: checking where the balance went.

Decision 2: choose the moment

Choosing a unit answers what users spend. Next comes when they learn about it.

There are three chances to communicate cost: before, during, and after the work. Ignore them and the user finds out at a fourth moment: the wall, when the allowance runs out or an unexpected charge appears.

Before the work, help people judge the likely cost while they can still change the scope. Explain what drives it, use a range when the total is uncertain, and offer a cheaper mode, a smaller run, or a spending ceiling.

During the work, show meaningful progress instead of an unreliable countdown. Let long jobs run without keeping people on the same screen. Make it clear what stopping will cost, and ask before continuing if the original estimate no longer holds.

After the work, show what was delivered and what it cost. Explain unusual charges, make reused work or savings visible, say how failures are billed, and keep a history people can return to. These are the three moments the illustration brings together.

Before: model selectors, effort controls, and previews

Before a run begins, the user can still change the scope. Three controls are especially useful.

Model selectors. A dropdown of model names can force people into an engineering decision. Not everyone wants that. In August 2025, OpenAI launched GPT-5 with automatic routing, then quickly brought back clearer choices such as Auto, Fast, and Thinking alongside more detailed model controls. The lesson isn’t that model choice should disappear. It’s that most users benefit from an outcome-oriented default, while advanced users still need access to the underlying models.

Effort controls. Effort dials are becoming increasingly common in AI products, but what they actually control remains a mystery to many users. Cursor offers a scale from Low to Extra High, other interfaces use sliders, while deep-research modes make the choice more implicit. All give users some control over how much time and computation a model spends on a task. But what does High really mean compared to Medium? Will the result be noticeably better, take longer, or simply consume more of the user’s allowance? The controls are becoming more familiar, but the trade-offs behind them are still poorly explained.

Previews before large spend. Deep-research screen gives users a plan they can edit before an agent starts reading sources. That’s a strong moment to intervene. The two missing pieces are cost and consent. A plan with five steps doesn’t reveal whether cutting one will save much. And for a genuinely costly job, an auto-start countdown can turn doing nothing into agreement.

A good preflight makes the trade-off concrete: what’s included, what’s optional, what the approximate total could be, and what will happen if the job needs more.

Clay is a useful reference for pricing before execution. In the captured interface, enrichments show figures such as “0.5 / row,” “~3 / row,” or “varies by model.” A recurring signal displays its monthly cost before activation. These labels tell the truth about uncertainty rather than presenting every action as fixed-price.

The same principle applies to scheduled work. Show the likely monthly spend of an hourly or nightly automation, not just its price per execution. Small recurring charges are easy to overlook.

During: progress, cancellations, and changing forecasts

This is the thinnest part of many AI cost experiences. A run starts, a spinner appears, and all the useful controls return only when it’s finished.

Show real units of progress when they exist: 320 of 500 contacts processed, 12 sources checked, three files edited. For open-ended work, show meaningful phases instead of a percentage you’ve invented. Let long jobs move out of the foreground without losing their status.

Where costs accrue as the job runs, display usage so far and the remaining budget or cap. A forecast can change if an agent discovers extra work. When the expected cost moves well beyond the original range — or reaches an agreed checkpoint — pause and ask whether to continue. Don’t silently treat the original approval as unlimited permission.

After: receipts

The receipt connects a charge to the work it paid for. It’s also what helps people make a better choice next time.

  • Per action, right next to the result. Replit’s captured run summary lists “13 actions” and what changed; a message menu shows “Worked for 43s” and “Credits used 0.50.” The receipt is available where the work happened.
  • Per session, with cost drivers. Another captured panel shows 3,450 credits alongside context used by instructions, tools, messages, files, and tool results. The surprising insight isn’t the total; it’s what consumed the context. A Compact Conversation control gives the user a way to respond.
  • Per period, with searchable history. Clay’s usage history can be examined by time, column, run, or provider and exported. That’s what a team lead needs when someone asks why the workspace budget changed.

A breakdown with a way to act is a receipt. A breakdown without one is a report.

For most users, keep the first layer light. Put the deduction and result together; make the technical breakdown one click away; put exportable history where teams already manage billing.

Do: Attach a light receipt to the result, reveal cost drivers on demand, and record the failure policy.

Put it to work

As AI products move toward longer, more autonomous workflows, the cost of a single action becomes harder to predict. What looks like one request can involve dozens of steps, multiple models, and external tools. Traditional usage meters weren’t designed to explain that complexity.

The challenge isn’t simply to expose more information. It’s to help people understand what they’re spending, why costs vary, and which choices are within their control.

Across the examples we’ve explored, one principle stands out: cost should be visible when it matters, without becoming something users have to think about constantly.

Good cost transparency isn’t about making every charge predictable. It’s about making uncertainty understandable, so people can make informed decisions without needing to understand the system underneath.

This essay was originally published on my Substack Syntax Stream, where I write about principles of human–AI interaction.

title: Context is the new interface
text:
Context is the new interface

The future of design lies in what happens between products

Imagine you receive a message from a friend recommending a restaurant. You want to check where it is, see whether you are free that evening, and reply with a time that works for both of you. You search through your messages, open the link, check the location, switch to your calendar, return to the conversation, and finally write your reply.

Each step is simple on its own, but together, they create a fragmented experience. You have to carry the context from one product to another, remembering what you were doing and what you need to do next. This is a familiar interaction. We have designed products around individual tasks for years, leaving people to connect those tasks themselves. But when AI can interpret an intention and help carry it across products, the experience starts to change.

The question becomes how we design what happens between interfaces.

From applications to context

The app became the dominant model for digital experiences because it gave software a clear structure. Each product has its own interface, features, and way of managing information. People move between them to complete a task.

The problem is that people’s intentions rarely follow these boundaries. Planning a trip involves conversations, calendars, maps, bookings, and payments. Organizing a meeting requires information about people, availability, locations, and commitments that may live in several different systems.

Each product can work perfectly well on its own while the overall experience remains fragmented. AI makes it possible to approach these activities from another direction. Instead of asking people to identify the right application and navigate its features, an assistant can start with their intention and determine which information and capabilities are relevant.

Apple’s work on Siri and Apple Intelligence illustrates this direction. Through its App Intents framework, Apple allows developers to describe actions and content that can be made available to supported system experiences. This gives Siri and other supported features a structured way to discover what an application can do.

Imagine asking Siri to find a restaurant a friend recommended in an earlier conversation, check your availability for Friday, and help prepare a reservation. Depending on the available integrations and permissions, the assistant could connect information that would otherwise require several manual searches. The applications remain responsible for their data and functionality, but their capabilities can be accessed through an experience that begins somewhere else.

This changes the design problem, because the challenge is no longer limited to helping someone navigate an application. It also involves making the right information and capabilities available in the right context, at the moment they become useful.

For a practical explanation of how this works, Apple’s developer documentation on Apple Intelligence, Siri, and App Intents describes how app entities, schemas, and onscreen context help the system interpret and use app capabilities.

Context is a design material

Context has always been part of UX. It helps a system understand what a person is trying to do, what information is relevant, and what should happen next. It can include the current conversation, a person’s preferences, previous decisions, or the state of an ongoing task. It can also include constraints, such as whether a calendar is available or whether an action requires permission.

When someone asks for a restaurant recommendation, the request alone may not be enough. The assistant may need to understand the occasion, the people involved, the location, the available time, and any preferences that matter. Some of this information may already be available. Other details may need to be requested.

Designing for context means deciding which information matters at each stage and how it should influence the experience. It also means deciding what should be remembered, what should be shared between products, and what should remain private.

Memory becomes particularly important when a task spans time or products. An assistant might remember that a friend recommended a particular restaurant, that Friday was the preferred evening, or that the user usually avoids noisy places. But remembering information is not the same as knowing whether it is still relevant. The system should be able to surface the context it intends to use, especially when that context influences a decision. Showing someone that a restaurant was recommended by a friend six months ago gives them an opportunity to confirm or correct the information before the assistant acts on it. Memory should help maintain continuity without turning past behaviour into an unquestioned assumption.

Unfortunately, context is rarely complete. A person may say, “Find somewhere nearby for dinner,” without specifying a budget, cuisine, or exact time. The system has to decide whether it has enough information to proceed or whether it should ask a question.

This has implications for how products structure their information. In Apple’s App Intents framework, developers define entities, parameters, and actions so that supported system experiences can understand what an application contains and how its capabilities can be used. These definitions influence whether a system can identify the correct item, interpret a request, and perform an action reliably.

These decisions shape the interaction as much as the interface does. They determine whether the experience feels relevant, whether the user understands what is happening, and whether the system can act without making assumptions that matter.

Context therefore becomes a design material in its own right. It is part of the structure that makes an experience coherent, and it needs to be structured, interpreted, and actively designed rather than simply collected.

UX governance defines the boundaries

When an assistant connects information and actions across products, someone needs to determine how that information can be used and what the system is allowed to do with it.

Consider an assistant arranging a meeting. It finds an available time, retrieves the participants’ contact details, and prepares an invitation. Should it send the invitation automatically, or ask for confirmation? Which calendar should it treat as authoritative? What happens if availability changes before the invitation is sent?

These are questions of UX governance: the shared principles and rules that determine how an experience behaves across products and contexts. Governance establishes who can access information, which actions can be delegated, when approval is required, and how mistakes can be identified and corrected. Without these shared rules, an experience that crosses several products can become inconsistent, even if each application behaves as intended.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a useful foundation for thinking about these responsibilities. Its four functions, Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, provide a way to identify risks, establish accountability, evaluate system behaviour, and manage issues over time.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is another relevant development. It provides a standard way for AI applications to connect with external tools and data sources. This creates opportunities for systems to work together, while making questions about access, permissions, and responsibility important parts of the design.

For designers, these questions are part of the experience itself. If an assistant can take action across products, the boundaries of that action need to be understandable. People should know what the system can access, which tools it intends to use, and when their approval is required.

This also means making tool use visible. When an assistant searches a calendar, retrieves information from a message, or sends a request to another service, people should have a way to understand what happened and why. The aim is not to expose every technical operation, but to provide enough information for people to follow the process and remain confident in the result.

Governance cannot sit with one design team alone. It requires collaboration between design, product, engineering, security, legal, and the teams responsible for the systems involved. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework Playbook can help translate these responsibilities into practical activities throughout the development process.

Designing for uncertainty

Even well governed systems can misunderstand context. An assistant might find a restaurant recommendation from six months ago and interpret it as a current preference. It might identify a date in a message but misunderstand which event it refers to. The information is available, but its meaning depends on circumstances the system may not fully understand.

This also affects how information is presented. People need enough visibility to understand what the assistant has inferred, which details it is using, and what it plans to do. They should be able to correct an assumption without having to restart the entire task.

A useful design must account for this uncertainty instead of treating every inference as fact. One practical approach is to distinguish between information explicitly provided by the user and information inferred from context. Another is to consider the consequences of an incorrect decision when determining how much confirmation is necessary.

A restaurant suggestion can be presented as an option, with a brief explanation of why it was selected. A booking should make the date, time, and party size clear before confirmation if those details have not already been authorized. A conflicting calendar entry may require a question rather than an automatic choice.

The same principle applies to how an assistant communicates its plan. Before carrying out a task that involves several steps, it can explain what it intends to do, which information it needs, and where the user may need to make a decision. For a simple request, this might require only a short explanation. For a more consequential task, it may mean presenting a sequence of actions and waiting for approval before proceeding.

Planning and visibility become especially important when the task continues across products. If an assistant is finding a restaurant, checking availability, and preparing a reservation, the user should be able to see what has been completed, what is still in progress, and what remains to be decided. Without this visibility, even a successful process can feel unpredictable.

For designers, the practical questions are straightforward. What does the system know, and where did that information come from? What assumptions is it making? What does it plan to do next? How costly would a mistake be? Can the user understand and correct the result?

These questions help teams design for the full journey, including moments when the system cannot confidently proceed, rather than treating uncertainty as an edge case. They also make the experience easier to understand and recover from when something goes wrong.

The product team no longer owns the entire experience

When a task moves across several products, no single interface necessarily contains the full experience. A user may begin in a conversation, use information from a calendar, rely on a recommendation service, and complete an action through another product.

Each product still has a role. Its value also depends on how well it participates in the wider journey. This changes the questions product teams need to ask. They need to understand which information their product makes available, which actions other systems can request, and how those actions fit into a task that may begin somewhere else.

This creates a different relationship between products and their users, because a product can contribute to a successful outcome without the person visiting its interface at all.

For product teams, that means app sessions and screen time are incomplete measures of value. A service might help someone complete a reservation through an assistant, even if the user never opens its home screen. This does not make interface design less important. It changes the scope of the work around it.

It also means that teams need to consider how their products communicate progress and responsibility to systems outside their own interfaces. If an action is started by one product and completed by another, the transition should not leave the user wondering what happened or who is responsible for the outcome.

The experience needs to remain coherent even when its parts belong to different teams. This requires shared expectations about what each product can do, how its actions are reported, and what happens when the next step cannot be completed.

What designers should work on next

Designers can begin by mapping the context a task requires. This includes the information a system needs, where that information comes from, how it changes over time, and which products are involved. They also need to define how the system should behave when context is missing, incomplete, or ambiguous.

Microsoft’s Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction provide a useful foundation for this work. Building on these principles, we can identify a set of recurring patterns for designing agentic experiences and workflows, regardless of their specific domain.

Planning and visibility

Teams need to decide when an assistant should explain its intended steps, when it should show progress, and how people can understand the status of a task that spans several products. The level of detail should depend on the complexity and consequences of the task. People need enough visibility to understand what the system plans to do, what it has completed, and what still requires their attention.

Memory surfacing

Designers should consider how the system uses past conversations, preferences, and decisions to inform the current experience. People need ways to understand which information is influencing a recommendation or action, and to correct it when it is outdated or no longer relevant. The aim is to provide continuity without turning past behaviour into an unquestioned assumption.

Tool use disclosure

When an assistant uses external tools or accesses information across products, people should be able to understand what it has accessed and which actions it has taken. Teams need to distinguish between a suggestion, an attempted action, and a completed outcome. This makes the system’s behaviour easier to understand and helps people know when they need to intervene.

Multi step workflow tracking

A task that spans several products should feel like a continuous journey rather than a series of disconnected operations. Designers can map its stages, the information passed between them, and the decisions that require user involvement. People should be able to see what has been completed, what is in progress, and what remains to be done without having to reconstruct the process themselves.

Recovery routing

Not every task will go as planned. An assistant may encounter missing information, a failed action, or a decision it cannot confidently make. Designers need to define how the system responds in these situations, whether by asking a question, returning to an earlier step, suggesting an alternative, or handing control back to the user. Recovery should preserve the context already established and help people continue without having to start again.

Autonomy

Teams also need to decide how much autonomy to give the system. Autonomy is not a choice between a fully manual experience and an assistant that does everything independently. It is a spectrum.

An assistant might suggest a restaurant without taking any action, prepare a reservation for review, or complete a booking once it has the necessary permission. The appropriate level depends on the task, the user’s preferences, the reliability of the available information, and the consequences of a mistake.

Designing for autonomy means making the transition from recommendation to preparation and action understandable. People should be able to delegate routine steps while retaining control over decisions that matter to them. They should also be able to change their minds, interrupt a process, or take over when the system reaches its limits.

Testing

Testing should follow the task across products. Instead of evaluating each interface separately, teams can examine the full journey from the initial request to the final outcome. They can test what happens when information is unavailable, the system makes the wrong assumption, an action fails, or a user changes their mind. This helps reveal gaps between products that may not be visible when each interface is tested in isolation.

Collaboration

Designing these experiences requires collaboration across product boundaries. Designers need to work with engineers and other teams to understand system capabilities, data access, permissions, and limitations, then translate these constraints into experiences people can understand and trust.

The aim is to make the connections between products feel coherent while keeping the underlying actions visible, understandable, and under the user’s control.

Beyond the interface

The restaurant example began with a simple recommendation. Completing the task required information, decisions, and actions that lived across several products. As AI systems become able to work with more of these connections, the experience will depend on how well context is carried from one step to another.

The design challenge is to make that process useful, understandable, and respectful of the boundaries between systems. People need to know what the assistant remembers, how it plans to proceed, which tools it uses, and what happens when a task cannot be completed as expected. They also need control over how much they delegate and the ability to step in when necessary.

Interfaces remain where people see, guide, and correct what is happening. But more of the experience is shaped by the context that surrounds them, the decisions a system makes, and the rules that determine what it can do.

Designing for this future means looking beyond individual screens and considering the relationships between products. It means treating context, memory, planning, permissions, recovery, and governance as part of the experience from the beginning.

The future of design lies in what happens between products.

References

  1. Apple Developer Documentation. Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. Technical guidance on exposing app content and actions, transferable entities, schemas, and onscreen context to Siri and Apple Intelligence.
  2. Apple Developer Documentation. Getting started with the App Intents framework. An introduction to making app actions and content available outside the app through system experiences.
  3. Apple Developer Documentation. Providing contextual cues to Apple Intelligence and Siri. Guidance on associating app entities with onscreen content so that Siri can interpret contextual references.
  4. Techstrong AI article on the MCP AI governance gap. The article highlights issues enterprises need to address as they connect AI systems with tools and organisational data.
  5. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0). A voluntary framework for managing AI risks and supporting trustworthy AI systems.
  6. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). NIST AI RMF Playbook. Practical suggestions aligned with the framework’s Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions.
  7. Amershi, S. et al. (2019). Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Proceedings of the 2019 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems.
  8. Microsoft Research and Microsoft’s UX design for agents .

From AI × Taste

A monthly series exploring the economics of taste in the age of AI:

  • AI made everyone a creator, not a designer
    How AI made generation abundant, making design judgment and taste the new competitive advantage.
  • The organizational costs of low taste
    How weak design judgment compounds across products, teams and organizations.
  • Taste cannot be delegated

  • Designing for the Proxy

  • When the canvas starts acting, who’s really in control?

  • The economics of attention in the age of AI. When machines pay attention, what deserves ours?

title: The people using AI should set its strategy
text:
The people using AI should set its strategy

Practitioners know what good output looks like and should own the final call, with operations handling the plumbing.

Picture a researcher who drops 12 interview transcripts into a synthesis tool and gets a tidy theme and quote. She ran six of those interviews, so she knows within a minute nobody said it.

The manager who negotiated the contract wouldn’t have caught it, because some people lack the hands-on experience that judgment takes.

Design and research operations grew up handling licenses, consent forms, and vendor contracts. When artificial intelligence tools arrived, buying them became deciding what they’re for.

That’s backwards, because this isn’t like choosing Figma or other tools, where the same input gave the same output and a checklist could judge them.

Until the field shakes out, the people using these tools should be the directly responsible individuals for the strategy, owners answering for each decision. They know what to look for. Operations should own the plumbing that makes their choices safe.

Job listings already show the skills gap where some teams clearly don’t have the skills for this world and lack the initiative to follow the industry, which is sad:

  • Okta is hiring a Senior Design Operations Program Manager, Agentic Design who works in Claude Code and Cursor.
  • Yahoo posted a Design Operations Manager, Systems and AI Enablement role to own its tooling roadmap.
  • Etsy wanted a Director, Design Operations fluent in Claude and Cursor.
  • Mistral wants a Product Operations Manager (DesignOps) who automates the team’s coordination and reporting.

I’ve spent more than 20 years in UX as a player-coach and wrote uxGPT: Mastering AI Assistants for User Experience Designers and Product Management Professionals. This is like the early days of the web, when the people coming in didn’t understand the tools and made many poor decisions.

We should avoid repeating that mistake.

Count the Shadow Tools

The first sign strategy is being set outside operations is the shadow stack. In Microsoft’s 2024 Work Trend Index, 78% of people using artificial intelligence at work brought their own tools. In the State of Prototyping: Spring 2026 survey from UX Tools, 59.1% of designers had built their own tool, app, or utility with artificial intelligence in the previous six months.

Every shadow tool is a vote cast by someone who can tell good output from bad. It’s also a vote that operations doesn’t understand the tools.

Many operations teams are struggling, and they’re falling behind because they aren’t putting in the time to follow the trends. In The State of Research Operations, a December 2025 User Interviews study of 21 specialists, six questioned how many of their roles will survive.

I’m seeing some organizations rename these teams agent operations, because existing groups haven’t learned the tools or lack the skill sets.

This isn’t just about UX.

Across industries, teams are figuring out how to reorganize around artificial intelligence. In McKinsey’s The State of AI in 2026: On the Road to ROI, nearly three-quarters of high performers had redesigned workflows, against a quarter of others.

People who don’t know the tools get replaced by people who do because they understand how to use it for their workflows.

A 2023 Harvard Business Review interview with Karim Lakhani made it the title: “AI Won’t Replace Humans, But Humans With AI Will Replace Humans Without AI.”

Learn From Past Waves

In 1979, VisiCalc shipped for the Apple II, and buyers understood it in minutes. Peter Jennings, a co-founder of its publisher, recalls in VisiCalc 1979 finding Apple computers on managers’ desks at Tandy’s headquarters, bought to run the spreadsheet.

Tandy sold its own computers through Radio Shack, and its managers still went around them.

The managers knew what a budget model had to do, so they could judge VisiCalc in a few minutes.

Software as a service repeated the first pattern. In its 2019 Form S-1, Slack told investors that usage inside organizations typically started bottom-up. Slack spread team by team because whoever ran internal tools didn’t understand the use cases, or didn’t try to.

The early web showed the other side.

By decade’s end Jakob Nielsen had measured what big companies got wrong. In his 1999 article Who Commits the “Top Ten Mistakes” of Web Design?, the 10 largest U.S. companies averaged a 20% violation rate on his list, against 13% for the 10 most-visited sites.

The biggest budgets bought more mistakes than the people living on the web. Artificial intelligence tools are running both patterns at once, on a shorter fuse.

Name the Evaluation Gap

I call this the evaluation gap: the distance between the person who approves a tool and the person who can tell when its output is wrong. Generative tools carry more nuance: which model a tool runs, how it handles a long transcript, and whether it shows its sources.

Anyone lacking the expertise misses that nuance and the failures inside it.

In legal technology, a contract summary that drops an indemnity exception or doesn’t understand the difference between assignment and change of control reads fine to anyone who has never negotiated one.

Generative tools produce something plausible every time, and the errors hide in details only a practitioner checks.

Subject matter experts (SMEs), the people who know a domain because they do the work, carry the advantage. Anthropic’s preliminary June 2026 study of about 400,000 Claude Code sessions, Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise, found expert sessions reached verified success more than twice as often as novice ones. The authors credit domain expertise rather than coding skill. A product manager who knows the pricing model catches generated requirements that drop the enterprise tier’s usage cap. A designer who knows the design system spots the prototype that invents a fourth button style.

My history runs almost four years with generative tools and seven before that with other artificial intelligence. It tells me which outputs to check first on a new tool.

Stop Counting Seats

Operations teams measure what they can see: seats, spend, renewals, and logins. Those numbers fit a license and fail a strategy. Better ones come from SMEs, such as the share of synthesized claims that survive a check against the transcripts and the token cost of each finished study.

In the User Interviews study, eight specialists described tool management as a growing share of the job. Money is tight: 17 said their scope had grown, while 12 said budget, staff, or resources stayed flat or shrank.

The case — if the business can’t see business impact, that set of roles are eliminated.

Seats are giving way to tokens. In Gartner Predicts AI Coding Costs Will Surpass Average Developer’s Salary by 2028, from June 2026, Gartner says coding vendors are moving from seats to consumption pricing. Deciding which work deserves the priciest model takes someone who knows the work.

Tool bloat is the canary in the coal mine from past operations mistakes. Those mistakes are costing the field jobs, and operations teams have to own this before they have credibiity.

In the UX Tools survey, 53% of designers said too many tools were slowing them down. A stack that keeps growing means nobody with judgment decided what each tool is for, and that’s a competence problem for whoever owns it.

Operations can cut the count once SMEs say which tools earn their place because that’s their right.

Hand Operations the Plumbing

Operations still matters.

Peter Merholz made the case in Peter Merholz: How Agile Can Turn Designers Into Pixel Pushers, a 2020 Superside interview. “If you don’t pay attention to the operations, the wheels come off,” he said.

Artificial intelligence adds plumbing, including contracts and maintenance for tools and workflows practitioners build. Even after years in legal technology, I don’t want to be in charge of the contracts. I was on a team whose internal workflow application became a nightmare to maintain. So split decision rights along the evaluation gap:

  • Own the judgment. SMEs who use the tools are the DRIs for which ones the team adopts and what counts as acceptable output. They set strategy.
  • Run the plumbing. Operations handles security and privacy review, contracts and data boundaries, access, budget, and upkeep. They run the trains.
Practitioners should decide what good looks like, and operations should make it safe to find out.

Bad calls are coming, and someone has to own them. Many operations people perceive more influence over these choices than their experience supports, and setting strategy from that seat is running with scissors.

A researcher who picked a tool that invents quotes can explain the failure and fix the review step.

An operations manager who never ran a study can only cancel the contract and usually acts too slow in the process. Treat the arrangement as temporary, because we’re moving at the speed of light, and revisit ownership once the field settles as in all innovation cycles.

Conclusion

Tandy had its own computers to sell, and its managers still bought Apple IIs to run a spreadsheet. The official plan stopped mattering once the people doing the budgets had found a better tool. Design and research teams are there now, and the shadow stack is the evidence.

This is a good time to reevaluate operations teams the way we’re reevaluating design systems and other roles: what value they provide and what the job requires. UX, like every field, has to evolve toward fewer roles and more skills, because role titles are selfish: they protect turf rather than the work, and that’s hurting the field. The job growing underneath operations is the plumbing that lets good choices scale.

Practitioners have work to do, too. Owning strategy means writing down the quality bar, sharing tools that work instead of hiding them, and retiring ones that stop paying off. A designer who wants the decision must defend it in a budget review, with numbers about the work instead of the logins.

Picture that researcher again, the one who caught the invented quote in under a minute. Give her the decision, and give operations the job of making it safe to act on.

Action items

  • Write the decision charter. Name three to five SMEs who use artificial intelligence tools every week as the DRIs for which tools design and research adopt, renew, or drop, and make them answerable for the results. Put the split on one page, with operations owning security, privacy, contracts, access, token limits, and maintenance, and revisit it every six months while the field settles.
  • Build a task benchmark. Collect 10 real tasks with answers your team trusts, such as a coded interview or a finished flow, and run every candidate tool against them before anyone signs a contract, scoring errors caught, edits needed, hours saved, and token cost. Settle disputes over a tool with the results. It’s the kind of internal benchmark Ethan Mollick recommends in Making AI Work: Leadership, Lab, and Crowd.
  • Surface the shadow stack. Ask the team which personal tools they use and for what, promise there’s no penalty for answering, and treat the list as a shortlist for evaluation and a count of the bloat to cut.
  • Rewrite the operations job descriptions. Reevaluate what design and research operations is for, the way you would a design system, and hire or train for hands-on tool skills, token and budget governance, and vendor management alongside the contract work.
