title: How I stopped dreading AI and started studying it full-time
text:
How I stopped dreading AI and started studying it full-time

By June 2026, I couldn’t open an app without being told I was falling behind. My Instagram saves were full of designers building agents over a weekend. LinkedIn was a steady stream of people who had “shipped it with Cursor.” And the job listings I was tailoring my resume to kept asking for things like evals, MCP, AI prototyping and Claude Code: words I half recognized and could not have explained in an interview.

I could feel myself staring down a fork. Down one path was a designer I’d been before at times: only integrating new ways of working if my boss told me to do it, dreading every new tool launch, complaining about having to adapt and quietly missing the good old days. Down the other was someone who got excited about what was coming and went looking for it before anyone asked them to.

I realized that I wanted to be the second designer. And I didn’t want to just pick up enough vocabulary to survive a screening call.

I want to dive deep enough to really understand how all of this works, because I won’t be able to truly design confidently for a technology I don’t understand.

For this very big goal, I had to get serious about learning. I asked Muse (Meta’s AI agent, which had access to every post I’d saved on Instagram) to dig through my saved AI and design content and turn it into a handoff doc. I went back through the job listings I had tailored my applications to with Claude and pulled out every AI skill I was missing. Then I handed all of it to Claude and asked for a learning plan that would turn me into the designer I wanted to become.

I had one condition: everything had to be grounded in real sources. Influencer reels are great for finding out what exists, but I wasn’t going to learn an entirely new discipline from a couple of 30-second clips optimized for views. Therefore, I asked Claude to back every topic with at least one article from a trusted source.

What came back was intense: 8 weeks, 40 hours a week, two demo projects to build from scratch and a deadline of November 22. I would be my own manager and my own teacher, working alongside a growing cast of Claudes (one wrote the plan, one tutored me, one built code with me, one helped me journal), and of course I would ultimately be the experiment subject absorbing all of it.

I’ll be honest about why I’m doing this. I want to get hired, but more than that I want to be the best designer I can be, in a field that changes every time I refresh my feed. That takes discipline, and it takes a willingness to look somewhat stupid while I figure things out.

Three weeks in, I’ve been posting one story a week on LinkedIn. This article is a bit different: it pulls those weeks together by theme instead of by date, because the same lessons kept showing up again and again, in a different costume each week.

A plan for a user of one (me)

Unfortunately, the plan written for me has to actually be learned and absorbed by me. It turns out I had to work out how I learn before I could plan anything further.

Week 1 was mostly new vocabulary (agents, tool calls, context windows, evals), so the tutoring Claude built a mini lesson around every reading. It rewrote dense passages in plainer language (I will never be a real engineer), introduced one term at a time and quizzed me with “what would you do?” questions. I loved it, and I also overdid it. I didn’t know which parts mattered, so I took in everything in every format I could: reading it myself, reading Claude’s summaries, reading the plain-language rewrites, then listening to text-to-speech on my outdoor runs. Naturally, Week 1 ran 3 days over.

The plan doc itself needed a redesign, too. It started as one long page, and scrolling through the doc on a trackpad made my carpal tunnel act up. So I treated it like any product with a frustrated user: I complained in a productive way (a.k.a. gathering user pain points) and requested that Claude reformat the doc as one tab per week and a table per task, with a checkbox, the task and its sources, and a notes column.

In Week 2, I changed how I asked. Before touching the readings (Google’s People + AI Guidebook and Microsoft’s Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction), I asked Claude for a short list of what to focus on and a top-down summary of the week’s objectives, plus why each one mattered for me. Then I read both guides on my own, with no tutor wrapped around them, and took my own notes. My delay went from 3 days to 1, and I actually remember that material better than Week 1. Neither mode was wrong. Week 1 needed a tutor because everything was new, and Week 2 needed independence because I finally had something to build on.

What I learned is that the tool only fits me as well as I describe myself to it, so every prompt is really a small design brief. Of course it gets better each time it learns something new about the user (me).

Asking better questions also made me pay closer attention to the answers. And some of those answers were very wrong…

Checking the checker

If I had to sum up all 3 weeks in one phrase, it would be this: nothing and nobody is infallible, and everyone needs a checker (or rather “who watches the watchmen?”) Each week added another layer to check.

Layer 1: checking the work

In Week 1, I built a tiny AI agent that helps people find software their company has approved, and I tested it with evals: the same set of questions asked on every run, graded two ways. Plain code checked exact facts, like which tools the agent used, and a separate reviewer Claude read each answer for meaning. Then I changed one small example in the agent’s instructions, and something I never touched broke. Every code check still passed, but the reviewer Claude noticed that in 4 of the 6 answers about one product, the agent had stopped naming the seller. My tutoring Claude traced the cause to an older example in the instructions, one it had written itself, that left the seller out. The agent was copying that example, mistake and all (read about it on LinkedIn).

What I took away from this is success is entirely determined by the answer key.

I changed the key to where the seller’s name is now a permanent code check, and the reviewer Claude can read the agent’s answers but can’t edit anything. Only I can change the tests, because an AI that can edit both the work and the tests grading it can “pass” just by making the tests easier. (Researchers call this reward hacking, and it’s behind some of the AI “cheating” headlines I’d been reading.)

Layer 2: checking the checker checking me

In Week 2, I flipped it around. I gave Claude scrubbed files from a 2025 usability study I ran at AWS and asked it to synthesize them blind, so I could grade it against my own answer key. Claude credited quotes to the wrong participant twice and turned a neutral remark into an opinion. It also found two errors in my answer key, and one of my 2025 counts changed from 17 of 25 sessions to 18 of 26 (read more on LinkedIn).

Run 2 was real research: synthesizing 13 public forum posts about AWS Private Marketplace. This time I put my research question at the top and gave each source its own labeled section, because Run 1 had shown me what happens without them. All 24 quotes came back exact and credited to the right source. Claude still made mistakes, just a different kind: it stated guesses as facts, and it applied findings about AWS Marketplace in general to the much narrower Private Marketplace. (One of my own leads made the same leap too) Clean, labeled data fixed the quoting errors but left the reasoning errors, so I still check every run.

Layer 3: checking the plan writer

In Week 3, something I had taken for granted made a big mistake. I’m generally a fan of how Claude can turn a pile of information into a structure and plan I can digest. What I assumed was that when I hand it information, it actually reads all of it. Isn’t processing huge amounts of data supposed to be AI’s strength? My first demo project is a redesign of AWS’s developer documentation, and the plan-writing Claude had initially listed 8 problems with those docs for me to solve. When I went back to them, I noticed none had a source and all read like common heuristics. After a week of digging through forums for actual user feedback, I suspected that the planning Claude hadn’t done its due diligence.

So I redid the research in a separate chat with real complaints and a test of the live docs, causing a tidal wave of rescoping for the project. The research Claude kept a log of its own mistakes, including quotes it had pulled from a GitHub page that no longer exists. It also flagged sources that needed context: the harshest Hacker News quote came from the person launching the AI tool being discussed, and a 2019 post asking “Why is AWS documentation so poor?” was promoting a YouTube channel.

Even the plan I built this whole experiment on needed checking. That rescoping cost my previous days.

Layer 4: checking with counts

The last layer came from AWS’s own AI answer agent in its docs. When I tested whether it kept track of follow-up questions, one failed and one passed. Claude suggested wording it as “sometimes loses context.” But “sometimes” can’t be measured, so I asked for harder tests, and the result became 3 of 10 follow-up tests failing (as of Oct 15).

Then on Oct 21 I tested the AWS docs answer agent on follow-ups by asking it about “the third one” from a list of four encryption options it had just given me. Bafflingly, the agent pulled up the second option instead. I tested it twice more and got the fourth option both times: 0 of 3 right, with the same list on screen every time.

Claude suggested fixing this by adding a line of interface text, and I pointed out that no line of text can fix a wrong pick. So the fix moved into code: find item three in the visible list and hand it to the AI, the loading text names the item, and if code can’t tell which one I mean, the response will ask. Claude correctly noted out that this is the same rule as my Week 1 agent.

One test is an anecdote and a count is evidence, and the rules that really matter belong in code, where the AI can’t talk its way around them.

What AI can’t see

Not every miss has a clean explanation. Plenty came from Claude just messing up because it’s an imperfect computer program. But some of them I could trace back to a reason:

Claude can’t see what I see, because what I see comes from years of experience it doesn’t have.

The clearest example sat in Claude’s own screenshots. While planning my docs redesign, the planning Claude captured reference pages from AWS’s documentation and proposed a brand new “ask the docs” AI feature. Weeks later, I was annotating those same screenshots by hand when I spotted a “Search in this guide” box in the page header. I recognized the sparkle icon and gradient border right away, because years of designing with Cloudscape (AWS’s design system) taught me that it uses them only to mark an AI feature. TLDR; AWS already has an AI answer feature in its docs, and Claude didn’t see it at all. My demo went from “I invented an AI search feature” to “I tested a live AWS AI feature, found where it fails, and redesigned it”.

This wasn’t the first time. In Week 1, Claude assumed my second demo was a retail agent that handles product refunds (it took the word ‘marketplace’ in the wrong direction). It’s actually a rebuild of my AWS Private Marketplace work, where companies control which software their employees can buy, and refunds aren’t even something those buyers can act on. I pointed to proof via live AWS docs, and Claude learned its lesson to check in with me more often.

The strangest moment came in Week 3. I was designing what an AI answer should look like after a user stops it mid-response, and I asked Claude to show me what Claude itself does in that situation. It drew a proposal and then admitted it couldn’t draw its own interface correctly from memory, because claude.ai changes too often. So I took three rounds of screenshots of Claude working, Claude stopped before writing anything and Claude stopped mid-sentence, and showed the AI its own screen.

I was designing an AI feature by studying the AI I was designing it with, and it still needed me to be its eyes.

What ties these together is simple. Claude sees what’s written down and what it’s shown (via unlabeled screenshots usually). A lot of what makes me useful as a designer lives in my head: the visual language of a company I worked at, what actually shipped, which details matter to the people who use a product. Once I knew what Claude couldn’t see, I had a better idea of what parts only I could do.

Knowing when (and when not) to use AI

The split I’ve landed on started out of frustration, before this plan existed. Back in August, I was doing a four-hour take-home assignment for a contract role interview and had just connected Figma to Claude for the first time. I asked Claude to take its own reference screenshots, and it couldn’t (the browser extension wasn’t connected, and its sandbox couldn’t reach the websites). So I did it all by hand. I took the screenshots, marked what worked and what didn’t with sticky notes in Figma, and handed those annotated boards to Claude as my wireframes to build four different website directions.

Two months later, Claude can take the screenshots itself but I still do the annotating. In Week 3 I pulled every screenshot into Figma and covered them in sticky notes. Each of the 9 docs problems got its own color, so I can see them zoomed out in a sprawling file, and each note gets a matching box around the exact element it’s about.

AI can now build, migrate and spin things up from nothing, and I’m happy to let it. But critique and pixel-level inspection are the core of my job as a senior designer.

The sparkle icon and gradient border only jumped out at me because I was the one looking closely, and because I knew what Cloudscape uses them for. AI can gather my annotations and group or transform them, but it can’t make them for me.

The opposite case came a few days later. By then, “Ask Docs” meant three different things across my docs: AWS’s live AI feature, my redesign of it and the first round of tests I ran. I knew this was exactly the kind of job AI does well (finding every instance of something, sorting each one by what it means and replacing all the names), so I handed it over with suggested names of my own. Claude made 28 changes in the research doc alone, and it caught two things I’d missed along the way.

It also suggested naming my redesign Grounded Answers. I hadn’t known “grounding” was an AI term (it means an answer comes from its sources), but it’s a word the AI practitioners interviewing me will know, so I took it. OK, Claude!

And sometimes the right tool isn’t AI at all. My redesign assumed most developers search the docs first, the way I do. Instead of asking Claude whether that was true, I texted a former coworker who’s a senior engineer. He sent back: he does a search first to find the area or topic, then lingers in the navigation to see related pages. He also told me AI reads most docs for him now, and he no longer checks its sources. I kept accurate source links in my design anyway, because the developers who do check need them, and losing their trust can be crushing for an AI product. One person isn’t research, so search-first stays a hypothesis. But one real person told me more than any confident paragraph from a model could.

Knowing what to hand off, what to keep and when to ask a human is the skill I’m practicing most. Once I understood that split, I could design better alongside Claude instead of around it.

AI as a design partner

Week 3 was my first real design work of the plan, and designing with Claude felt like working with an awkward but productive teammate: brilliant at some things, weirdly awful at others, and always ready to get stuff done.

The best test came over where my redesigned AI answers should live on the page. Claude recommended a resizable drawer on the right side of each docs page and cited Cloudscape (AWS’s design system, which I know like the back of my hand) to back it up. I pushed back over several rounds: I reasoned that the docs page already has two side panels, and a third would squeeze the content even more. When Claude then offered to move search into the existing (page-level) right panel instead, I said no for good. Search covers every guide and every service, so it belongs on the top header level, while side panels sit below the header and only show content for one page. Claude agreed, and then found its own test results backed me up: AWS’s AI feature already reads beyond the current guide. Claude knew the pattern rules. It took my information architecture sense to see which level the feature belongs on.

My reaction at the time: “wow my old Cloudscape reviewer eyes have not failed me yet, even a year out of practice.”

Other times it worked the way I’d want a good partner to. When I changed my mind about how to show that an AI answer might be wrong, I asked Claude the questions I couldn’t answer myself: should confidence be judged for the whole answer or for each section, and how much “why” should a user see? It came back with Amazon Bedrock’s grounding checks and HCI research, including a 2024 study from Microsoft Research with 404 participants. When an AI answer hedged in the first person (“I’m not sure, but…”), people agreed less often with its wrong answers and got more answers right overall (Kim et al., FAccT 2024). It also checked my mockup against the live Cloudscape rules and caught two real fixes.

And I had to learn to specifically ask for pictures. When I talk an idea through with a human designer/PM/engineer, someone can grab a pen and sketch it out. Claude can only draw through code, so its ideas arrive as walls of words. Now I ask it to “demonstrate visually” before I approve anything I can’t picture, and I only approve a change once I’ve seen it with my designer eyeballs.

By the end of the week, I’d written Claude a performance review. The short version: as a manager setting scope and requirements, Claude was supremely confident and frequently wrong. As a teammate doing the groundwork, it was far more trustworthy (as long as I set the scope). Asking simple questions out loud, like whether my research covered one AWS service or all of them, kept the scope from slipping more than once.

The part I keep thinking about is how easily Claude agrees with me. When I make an executive decision it almost always goes along with it, which spares me from upsetting several levels of stakeholders over a hunch. It also means I could bully it into agreeing with almost anything.

I’m an honest person trying to actually retain everything I’m learning so I’m not going to sweep away inconvenient feedback. This is the same discipline that got me started grinding on this plan in the first place.

Me and AI

Some learnings are already leaking out of the plan and into my everyday tasks. In Week 1 I learned how the context window works: when a chat runs too long, Claude gets worse at the task and burns through more tokens. So I wrote it into my account-level instructions, and now Claude tells me when it’s time to start a fresh chat. I’ve used that rule to hand off this very journal more than once.

Other lessons are about what I won’t hand over. This week, I asked Claude to make the graphic for my Week 3 post (see the report card above). It built a clean, tidy performance review form, and I liked the report card idea, but the result looked way too AI-made. I wanted something scrappy and imperfect, so I took the idea and remade it myself in Figma.

The same goes for writing. I’ve asked Claude to help draft my posts, but none of them ever sound quite right.

I realized that AI can only work from sampling the work of past me, but I as a person am always evolving. I am always adding something new to how I write and talk, from whatever I’m reading, learning or living through that week. No context window can hold all of me.

When Claude writes, it treats me as a formula and fills in any gaps with patterns from other people’s writing. Of course my voice gets diluted. This article started as a Claude draft too, and every sentence you just read went through copious rewrites from my carpal-tunnel-plagued hands before it settled here.

This brings me back to where I started. I took on this plan to become a designer who understands AI well enough to know what to give it, what to check and what to keep. Three weeks in, the most valuable thing I’ve built is a shift in habits: be curious about new things, and trust none of it until I’ve checked it for myself.

In Week 4, I’m building my redesign in real code with Cloudscape components and setting up evals to test it against AWS’s live feature. I’ll keep posting one story a week on LinkedIn, and the next theme article comes after Week 6.

If you’re a designer learning AI right now: what’s the part of your work you’ve vowed never to hand over to a fancy computer program?

Further reading

The basics

  • Building effective AI agents, Anthropic (2024). The Week 1 reading that taught me what an agent actually is.
  • Context windows, Claude docs. Why long chats get worse, and why Claude now tells me when to start a new one.
  • What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?, modelcontextprotocol.io. One of those job-listing words, explained by the people who made it.

‘’A plan for a user of one’

  • People + AI Guidebook, Google PAIR.
  • Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, Microsoft Research (CHI 2019). The 18 guidelines behind the HAX Toolkit, and my other Week 2 reading.

‘Checking the checker’

  • Demystifying evals for AI agents, Anthropic (2026). How to test an agent with the same questions every run.
  • Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning, Lilian Weng (2024). A deep dive into why an AI that can edit its own tests shouldn’t be trusted to.

‘What AI can’t see’

  • Ingress, Cloudscape Design System. The rule behind the sparkle icon I spotted: “Sparkles are the symbolic convention for generative AI.”
  • Colors: Gradients, Cloudscape Design System. The rule behind the gradient border, which is reserved for “elements that represent a generative AI entity.”
  • Generative AI patterns, Cloudscape Design System. The full set of chat, loading, follow-up and regeneration patterns I designed with.

‘AI as a design partner’

  • Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses, Amazon Bedrock docs. How AWS checks whether an answer actually comes from its sources.
  • “I’m Not Sure, But…”: Examining the Impact of Large Language Models’ Uncertainty Expression on User Reliance and Trust, Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard and Wortman Vaughan, FAccT 2024. The 404-person study on AI that hedges in the first person.

My weekly LinkedIn posts

  • Week 1: the regression my evals caught
  • Week 2: the blind test that graded me too
  • Week 3: Claude’s performance review
  • My Week 1 agent’s code, GitHub

I’m Lisa Liu, a senior product designer based in NYC, most recently at AWS Marketplace and AWS Data Exchange. This is the first theme article in my Teaching Myself AI With AI series. Currently available for senior IC and design lead roles. Portfolio at lisanianliu.framer.ai.

Find me on LinkedIn or at lliu29@yahoo.com.

title: The AI reckoning in UX was 20 years in the making
text:
The AI reckoning in UX was 20 years in the making

Everyone thinks AI is coming for design. The truth is uglier and older. The field has done this to itself twice before, and it’s about to do it again.

The UX job market right now is genuinely grim.

Jeff Sauro, PhD and Jim Lewis, PhD found that UX job postings are down 71 percent from their 2022 peak, and research postings are down even further. They also found that one in three organizations cut UX staff in a single year, the worst reading on record, worse than the one right after the 2008 financial crisis.

When companies trimmed their teams, UX roles took a bigger share of the cuts than their headcount would predict. Open your feed on any given day and someone talented is announcing they’re leaving the field, or asking if they should.

The excuse used to explain it is that AI came for us. The tools got good, the machines can design now, and a generation of designers is being automated out of a job they’ve spent their careers training for. In the more than 120 articles and discussions from the UX community that Prakash Shukla and his colleagues analyzed, they found that the automation anxiety, the fear of being de-skilled and replaced, ran through all of it.

Let’s cut the crap. This exact same thing has happened twice before.

What’s happening to UX is real, and it’s painful, but it is not the story people think it is. This is the third time the field has blown up, pulled in a flood of people chasing a hot job, and then contracted hard and squeezed a lot of them back out.

It happened when the dot-com bubble burst. It happened again when the bootcamps turned “UX designer” into a twelve-week certificate. And it’s happening now. AI is only the latest version of a test the field keeps failing to prepare people for, and the most efficient one yet.

AI democratized output, but it did not do the same for expertise, and producing something has never been the same as knowing whether it’s any good. The same point, aimed at our own profession, gets far less flattering when you truly examine it up close.

The uncomfortable truth underneath this reckoning is that the industry spent twenty years teaching an enormous number of people that design is how something looks, and now we live in a reality where AI is very, very good at making things look finished.

Before everyone agrees the robots did this, though, it’s worth being honest about who actually built the thing the robots are now exposing.

We have done this exactly twice before

In the dot-com bust, I sat front and center watching the bloodbath, and while a lot of us saw it coming, it was not a pretty sight.

In the late nineties, the web was the gold rush, and “information architect,” which is what we called UX designers then, the person responsible for how a product actually works and how someone moves through it, not just how it looks, was suddenly a job you could get paid absurd money to do.

The big interactive agencies were hiring anyone who could spell HTML. The one I worked at was part of a wave of consultancies that got enormous by swallowing other agencies, and the whole industry was copying each other by hiring fast, billing faster, and not asking too many questions about whether the people flooding in actually knew the craft.

Why would they? The money was real and the work was getting shipped.

Then the bubble burst. The agencies that had ballooned on hype collapsed in spectacular fashion, and the layoffs were brutal and everywhere. At twenty-five years old, I witnessed a lot of people lose those jobs and felt something close to relief. A bunch of them, I told myself, were never really designers. They’d shown up for the money, they couldn’t do the actual work, and the crash was just sorting that out.

I was half right, and wholly a jerk.

The part I had right is that a boom really does pull in a lot of people who can’t yet do the actual job, which was never making the screens but knowing which ones were right and why. The part I had wrong is that it wasn’t their fault, and losing your livelihood is not a moral verdict on your talent. The pattern was real, however, and it would happen all over again soon enough.

The second time was the bootcamps. Starting around the early twenty-tens, a whole industry sprang up promising to turn anyone into a UX designer in a matter of weeks. It grew at a staggering rate, by one count the coding and design bootcamp industry grew 138 percent in a single year, minting tens of thousands of graduates and turning into a nine-figure business almost overnight.

The pitch came across as irresistible.

Twelve weeks to a certificate, a portfolio, and a six-figure job.

Schools advertised that the overwhelming majority of their students were placed within ninety days.

For a while, during the zero-interest-rate boom, companies were hiring designers as fast as they could find them, and it mostly worked. Graduates really were getting hired.

Then it didn’t.

When the market tightened, the same bootcamps started laying off their own staff, pausing programs, and in some cases shutting down entirely. The graduates they’d minted were suddenly competing for a shrinking number of junior roles against laid-off veterans, and a twelve-week certificate turned out to be useless protection as the tide went out.

None of this was a secret while it was happening. In the middle of the bootcamp boom, there was dissonance in the UX community that the model was broken, that teaching UX in a few weeks produced people who had the vocabulary but not the judgment, that hiring off certificates and portfolios was selecting for exactly the wrong thing, and that when the tools inevitably changed, the fundamentals, such as research, information architecture, and knowing why a layout works, that the fast track skipped, would be the only thing that still mattered.

The warnings were right in our faces, but the industry kept hiring off cheap and inexperienced portfolios anyway.

The thread connecting both waves has nothing to do with the people necessarily being bad at the job (though some arguably were).

Twice now, a hot field pulled in a flood of people and sold them the same bill of goods, that there was a fast, almost effortless way into UX, and a golden ticket waiting at the end of it. And twice now, when the correction came, those were the people it took first.

This wasn’t because they were frauds, but the reality they’d been swindled into was the version a downturn could most easily do without.

This brings us to the third wave, and to the uncomfortable question of what, exactly, the field has been teaching people design is.

What we taught people design was

There’s some real data on the problem that the field actually taught all those people who rushed in.

When Figma surveyed designers for its State of the Designer report, it asked them to define “craft,” you know, what we call the heart of what gives us passion for what we do and what creates great design.

The most common answer, from 58 percent of them, was visual polish. How it looks. Far fewer named the things that actually make a product work, like solving the real problem, understanding the person using it, the judgment to know what matters.

That’s bananas.

This is the tool company’s own data, drawn from its own users, and a majority of the profession defines its core skill as decoration.

That is not an accident, and it is not those “designers’” fault. It’s what they were taught, hired for, and ultimately rewarded for. The bootcamps that minted them sold a promise that you could learn the tools, the layouts, the components, the whole job, in twelve weeks, and come out a seasoned professional.

What twelve weeks can’t teach, which should have been obvious, is the years of watching real people struggle with real products that judgment actually comes from.

Sarah Doody, who has coached designers through their careers for two decades, sees the result constantly, and it isn’t limited to juniors. She describes experienced designers, people with a decade or more on their résumés, who still can’t build a layout with a clear hierarchy or walk into a room and ask the business question that actually matters.

Patrick Neeman has argued for years that the real value has always been in the strategic thinking the production was standing in for. For a long time, that didn’t cost anyone anything, because the job was mostly making screens. You could make things look finished all day, and nobody ever made you prove you knew why.

Things changed though. Google’s UX certificate, with more than 1.5 million enrollments, has become one of the most common ways people now enter the field, and it teaches the software and the deliverables, because that’s what fits in a syllabus, while quietly skipping the part that takes years.

Knowing whether the work is any good is the one thing you can’t shortcut, and the one thing nobody teaches.

This is where we are today, and it’s why this wave hits harder than the last two. A whole generation got taught that design is how something looks, and all of a sudden that’s exactly what AI does well.

Every wave runs the same test, and AI grades harder

Both of those crashes went after the same people. The ones who could only do the production. In the dot-com bust it was offshore shops and templated sites that made them replaceable. With the bootcamps it was simpler, the ones who only ever learned the software, without true strategic chops, couldn’t do anything the market still needed.

Now it’s AI, and it’s the most brutal one yet, because the one thing it’s genuinely great at is creating what appears to be a polished, ready-to-hand-over deliverable.

Ask Milli Vanilli how that works out. The act looked flawless right up until they had to sing live, and then reality hit. The backing track skipped and their whole veneer fell apart in front of everybody.

The split even shows up in the government’s own numbers. In their 2024 to 2034 projections, Michael Rieley and Javier Colato expect graphic design, the part of the field that’s mostly about how things look, to grow about 2 percent over the decade. Nearly flat, 457th out of 832 occupations they tracked. They name it directly as one of the jobs generative AI is already dampening.

Meanwhile the computer and mathematical work, the problem-solving side, is projected to grow 10 percent, and five of the fifteen fastest-growing occupations in the country, data scientists, information security analysts, and research scientists among them, sit in that group.

If you put those two numbers next to each other, the field is actually splitting.

AI does the good-looking part, the clean mockups and slick screens, well enough and cheap enough now that nobody pays a person just to do that.

This is why the survivors of this wave look so different from the casualties. The designers keeping their jobs are the ones who can walk into a review and say they figured out the team was solving the wrong problem, or that a change they fought for moved retention, in numbers, for a reason they can explain.

The people deciding who gets cut aren’t opening your Figma files to admire them. They’re asking what you actually changed about the business, and a lot of beautiful portfolios have no answer. Alex Williams makes the case that the designers who stay are the ones who can show their work moved a real number, conversion, retention, support load, in language a CFO reads fluently.

None of that is a life sentence, at least not yet. The dividing line AI is drawing runs between people who were taught to produce and people who learned to think. That line leans toward the idea that the thinking can be learned by anyone willing to do the unglamorous work.

Perhaps, this is what the field should have been teaching the whole time.

The fundamentals were always the job

It would be easy to end this by blaming AI, but that’s ignorant and wrong.

AI didn’t do any of this. It didn’t sell a twelve-week path to a career, hire designers for their dribbble shots, or build a cottage industry of certificates for tools instead of courses in how people think. Our industry did all of that, over twenty years, and AI is just the new guy coming in trying to be as helpful as possible.

Being angry at the tool is like being angry at the alarm clock.

The thing to take from this is not despair, because the numbers don’t support despair.

The work isn’t going away. It’s merely sorting itself out and the part of design that was always decoration is flattening out, the part that was always about thinking is still growing.

Kate Moran, Raluca Budiu, and Sarah Gibbons state that the fundamentals of good design don’t change, but the stakes are rising, and the people who thrive will be the ones who treat UX as strategic problem solving instead of a pile of deliverables.

Once again, design is being asked to prove it was ever more than decoration.

Even Jakob Nielsen, who helped invent this field, lands in the same place. Once AI handles execution, he argues, the whole bottleneck moves to judgment, and the only people who should feel threatened are the ones who defined their skills narrowly and low.

AI is a threat in exact proportion to how little thinking your job required.

If you’re wondering whether that certificate on your LinkedIn is worth the time, it isn’t. The UX Design Institute’s State of UX Hiring report, built on more than 500 hiring managers and practitioners, found that what gets you hired is the portfolio and the thinking you can show, not the credential you collected. A certificate can teach you the tool, but so can a YouTube video. Bootcamps can’t teach you whether what you made with any tools is actually good or smart, and that is what matters to the best people hiring in the industry.

What a certificate and AI can’t do for you is clear direction. You, a human, need to be able to look at the research, the problem, the half-built thing in front of you, and say strategically where it should go and why.

Jessica S. Hall tells designers to stop taking orders. Take what’s in front of you, figure out what the problem actually is, and propose a way forward instead of waiting to be handed one. The ones who get cut are usually the ones still waiting for the brief.

The work that survives is the oldest and least glamorous stuff in the field. Understanding the person you’re designing for. Knowing why one layout guides someone and another loses them.

Walking into a room full of executives and connecting a design decision to something the business actually cares about. Christine Haskell has written that in every one of these shifts, production gets easier while judgment gets more valuable, and that the craft was never reducible to the techniques a tool can now copy.

Sarah Doody keeps hammering the same thing: the designers who last never stopped developing their own judgment and refused to let a tool think for them. None of it is new. It’s what the best designers were always doing, and it survives every one of these waves because it’s the part no tool has learned to fake.

I say “we” through all of this on purpose, because I’m part of the field that let it happen, and twenty-five-year-old me, who felt relief watching people lose their jobs had plenty to learn too.

Whether you like it or not, the point of saying it out loud is to be honest that we built a version of this profession that was always going to get a bill, and to push, loudly, back toward the fundamentals that would have protected people in the first place.

For over twenty years, the field did a remarkable impression of the emperor’s new clothes. Everyone agreed the work was magnificent and nobody wanted to be the one to say a lot of it was decoration over nothing, and the longer it went on, the more expensive it got to admit.

AI is just the kid in the crowd saying the obvious thing out loud.

Every one of these waves clears out the same thing, and it does hurt. It’s the people who were sold decoration and told it was design. And every one keeps the same thing: the people who can actually do the work. AI is only frightening if what you were trained to sell was how it looks. If you learned how to think, it’s a very fast assistant.

The fundamentals were always the job. They still are. The sooner the field admits it taught people otherwise, the sooner it can start teaching them right.

References and further reading

The reckoning

  • Jeff Sauro and Jim Lewis, How Does the UX Job Market Look? (MeasuringU). The hard numbers behind the downturn: UX postings down 71 percent from their peak, and one in three organizations cutting UX staff in a single year.
  • UX Design Jobs and AI Displacement (Jobs After AI). On how UX roles took a larger share of cuts than their headcount would predict.
  • Prakash Shukla and colleagues, De-skilling, Cognitive Offloading, and Misplaced Responsibilities (arXiv). An analysis of more than 120 UX community articles and discussions, finding automation anxiety running through all of it.

We have done this before

  • The Last Big Tech Layoff Bloodbath: the Dot-Com Bust of 2000–2001 (SFist). A retrospective on the crash that cleared out the first wave.
  • Don Norman and Jakob Nielsen, The Definition of User Experience (Nielsen Norman Group). The original definition of UX from the people who coined the term.
  • The MarchFirst Autopsy (Unicorn Burn). How the dot-com roll-up giants grew huge and collapsed.
  • Coding Bootcamp Market Data (Course Report). The bootcamp boom, including the 138 percent single-year growth.
  • Coding Bootcamp Outcomes (SwitchUp). Placement data from the boom years, when graduates really were getting hired.
  • Bootcamps Are Dying (Datastream). The collapse: bootcamps laying off staff, pausing programs, and shutting down.
  • UX Design (Interaction Design Foundation). A reference on the fundamentals the fast track skips.
  • CFPB Takes Action Against BloomTech (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau). The federal action against a flagship bootcamp for misrepresenting its placement rates.

What the field taught

  • State of the Designer (Figma). The survey in which 58 percent of designers defined craft as visual polish.
  • Sarah Doody (Career Strategy Lab). On experienced designers who never built the judgment underneath the polish.
  • Patrick Neeman, What UX Competencies in a Generative AI World Could Look Like. On moving from pixel-pushing to strategic thinking.
  • Google UX Design Certificate (Coursera). The 1.5-million-enrollment credential that teaches the software and skips the years.

Every wave runs the same test

  • The Rise and Fall of Milli Vanilli (CBC). The act that looked flawless until the track skipped live.
  • Michael Rieley and Javier Colato, Industry and Occupational Employment Projections, 2024–34 (Bureau of Labor Statistics). The government projections showing graphic design nearly flat while the problem-solving work grows.
  • Alex Williams, Building a UX ROI Case That Survives the Boardroom (Smashing Magazine). On why the designers who stay can show their work moved a real number.

The fundamentals were always the job

  • State of UX Hiring Report (UX Design Institute). Research across 500-plus hiring managers finding that the portfolio and the thinking matter more than the credential.
  • Jessica S. Hall, Don’t Want to Be an Order Taker? Stop Taking Orders (Hallway). On proposing a direction instead of waiting to be told what to do.
  • Kate Moran, Raluca Budiu, and Sarah Gibbons, State of UX (Nielsen Norman Group). On the fundamentals holding while the stakes rise, and strategic problem solving winning out over deliverables.
  • Jakob Nielsen, Predictions for 2026. On the bottleneck moving to judgment once AI handles execution.
  • Christine Haskell, Broken Succession. On how production gets easier while judgment gets more valuable in every one of these shifts.

title: Monica Veloz Wants You to Grieve Out Loud
text:
Monica Veloz Wants You to Grieve Out Loud

I consider myself a pretty private person. I’m a journalist. My job, as my j-school professors drilled into my head, is to tell other people’s stories, not mine. On social media, I mostly post career highlights, leaving my romantic relationships and other intimate details of my life a mystery. It’s intentional. It’s protective. It’s how I want it. And maybe some of it is cultural. After all, Latinas are often taught not to air our dirty laundry in public. And yet, come July 2027, some of the darkest and hardest moments of my life will be sitting on a bookstore shelf near you. 

My debut memoir, The Best Love Stories Are Between Friends, will be out in the world, and in its pages, strangers and relatives will read about experiences I never shared with anyone. Why? Because the grief of losing my best friend, Angelica Alvarez, to stage 4 small-cell carcinoma lung cancer four years ago nearly killed me, too. And talking about her, our friendship, and the life-affirming power of girlfriends that sustain us, even in their death, is what helped pull me back to life. 

Sometimes, shamelessly allowing our grief to be seen, even in a culture that tells us to suffer in silence and move on, is what helps us carry it, and what allows those around us to carry theirs, too.

Monica Veloz, aka Monicastylemuse, understands this, too. The beloved Dominican-American content creator and beauty influencer is used to being honest about the challenges she faces as an Afro-Latina or her journey through motherhood. So when her own mother, Mama Muse, died of stage four gastric cancer, she mourned publicly, out loud, as her community of more than 400,000 followers on Instagram and Youtube (respectively) bore witness. 

In this episode, we speak with Monica about losing her favorite person, the loneliness of grief, and what it means to mourn out loud and in public without shame or fear of judgment. We explore the power of grieving on your own terms, honoring your loved ones unapologetically, and finding ways to keep those relationships alive long after death.

title: I Was Never Allowed To Go To Camp. So I Signed Up In My 30s
text:
I Was Never Allowed To Go To Camp. So I Signed Up In My 30s

Growing up, I watched films like The Parent Trap and It Takes Two, ‘90s classics where twin protagonists meet at summer camp and carry out shaving-cream and water-balloon pranks amid the most exciting cabin wars. I wanted so desperately to go away to camp for myself, to play tug-of-war, toast marshmallows, and then whisper under covers to a group of girlfriends I only saw a couple weeks every summer. And even though my Puerto Rican mother sat on the plastic-covered sofa next to me, also laughing when the identical characters fooled the adults around them into believing they were each other, she never budged when I’d beg her to sign me up for a camp experience of my own. 

“No, hay hombres,” she’d say, rejecting my pleas on the same grounds she’d use to deny my requests to sleep over at my friends’ houses, too. There were men there. Men she didn’t know. Men she couldn’t protect me from if I was miles away from her. 

I don’t blame Mami. According to research published in the peer-reviewed Trauma, Violence, & Abuse Journal in 2025, 3.7% of surveyed adults report experiencing child sexual abuse in youth service organizations, like summer camps, sports clubs, and religious organizations. Now as an adult, and an aunt, aware of the data and headlining stories, I understand and agree with Mami’s decision. But that understanding hasn’t quelled my inner child, still longing to spend a few days or weeks in nature, making camp friends and experiencing carefree fun and adventure. And now, I have the agency to make that choice for myself. So in July, I treated Baby Quels and signed up for Camp Elevate, an adult camp experience curated by Chase and Marriott Bonvoy to explore the benefits of the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card.

Our camp experience began at Trailborn Highlands, a cozy mountain lodge tucked into 4.5 wooded acres in North Carolina’s Blue Ridge Mountains. At roughly 4,100 feet above sea level, the air was a crisp 70 degrees and smelled of pine needles. I couldn’t wait to get outside and explore the forest like Annie or Hallie in The Parent Trap. Throughout the adult camp trip, I got to experience the perks Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card members could enjoy, both inside and outside the hotel. Just staying at the Trailborn Highlands and dining at the Highland Supper Club, which makes delicious vegan substitutes for its southern cuisine, can earn cardholders up to 17x total points to redeem toward future free nights. And new Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® cardmembers can earn even more Free Night Awards for stays valued up to 50,000 points each. 

During our first outdoor adventure, I joined my campmates, a group of journalists and publicists, for a guided hike through the lush Nantahala National Forest to Glen Falls. Along the way, we sampled the lemony leaves of sourwood trees and learned about the American chestnut, once a defining presence in these forests before a fungal blight decimated the species in the early 1900s. As we made our way deeper into the woods, the sound of rushing water grew louder until we reached overlooks offering views of the falls cascading over rugged rock formations, refreshing mist cooling us down from the hike. 

I stood amid the towering trees, taking it all in, grateful for the younger body that carried me up the trail and the older, more mature mind that knew to pause and appreciate the beauty around me. With its abundant rainfall and variety of plant and animal life, Highlands is one of the most biodiverse temperate regions in the world. It’s a breathtaking landscape shaped by nature and generations of people, including the Southern Blue Ridge Hikers, who guided our trek and help maintain local trails. The area also has a long history of conservation. In 1909, local residents rallied to protect the summit of Satulah Mountain from development, laying the groundwork for what would become North Carolina’s oldest land trust. Today, that legacy continues through community stewardship, donations, and visitors (like us) who support local conservation efforts.

When I returned to my room at Trailborn Highlands, I showered and welcomed a local massage therapist, who set up her table near the balcony overlooking the treetops. For an hour, she worked the knots and tension in my back, neck, and shoulders, discomfort that accumulated after years of work and stress. Baby Quels may not have known how to care for them, but Adult Quels was more than grateful for the reset, especially after nearly tapping out during the hike back.

Later that night, I got to return to treating my inner child, experiencing the camp activities I only ever saw on TV before then. First up was the Blue Ridge Cyanotype, a hands-on photography workshop at the hotel that uses light-sensitive paper to capture the shapes of leaves and flowers. We arranged our botanicals on the paper, placed them under a special light, and then submerged the prints in water to reveal delicate silhouettes against a deep-blue background. I made two prints, one I had framed and stands proudly in my home office, reminding me of a childhood dream finally realized. The experience costs $25 per person and earns Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card holders 17x points. Next, we headed to the outdoor patio to make s’mores. As a vegan, I built mine with plant-based marshmallows and chocolate sandwiched between graham crackers. It was my first time making them, and I felt a little giddy as I held my stick over the fire, rotating the marshmallow and getting a bit nervous when the heat hit my hands. It felt like the entire group turned into younger versions of ourselves, laughing, excited over kid camp treats, and attempting to swap scary campfire stories. 

The next morning, I made my way to Dixon Woods for an experience I’d long wanted to try: forest bathing. For two hours, Dr. Mark Ellison, founder of Pinnacle Forest Therapy and a certified forest therapy guide who leads experiences in the Highlands area, guided me through a practice of slowing down and reconnecting with nature. We sat and meditated as he shared poems by Mary Oliver and David Wagoner, writers whose words remind us that we, too, belong to the natural world. Then we wandered through the forest, bathing our senses in the landscape and taking time to focus on what we could see, hear, smell, and feel. With each pause, I focused on something new, from the velvety moss carpeting parts of the forest floor to the music of the songbirds soaring above me. We eventually returned to the ground to reflect on the experience and closed our time together with cups of white pine tea and a conversation about what nature had given each of us that day.

But the land had more to offer me. From Dixon Woods, we drove about an hour southwest to Rosman, North Carolina, for a special dinner at Rachel’s by the River, a rustic barn nestled along the French Broad River and operated by Headwaters Outfitters. I walked through the tall grass toward the river, watching the water tumble over the rocks. I listened to a live band play Appalachian bluegrass, swaying to the twang of the banjo and fiddle. I savored vegan renditions of a hearty spread of grilled apple-brandy “ribeye,” herb and sundried tomato couscous, miso-glazed mushrooms, and roasted sweet potatoes. 

Between the vista, live band, and food, I felt like I was in a scene I had only seen in a Hallmark film, you know, the ones where the big-city girl finds love in a small town and leaves the hustle and bustle of her career back home for the simple life. The love I discovered at Rachel’s by the River, and at camp overall, wasn’t romantic, but it was communal, the kind that keeps kiddies excited to return to camp every year.

As fall settles in, the crisp air and autumn leaves make me nostalgic for my time at camp, longing to return outdoors, to the simple joys of nature. I remember watching the sunset that last night and how my campmates and I ended our trip by singing Camp Rock’s “This Is Me” — just as we would have if it was 2008, when the Disney Channel classic dropped, when we were all still teens just imagining camp days like this one.

text:
Nina Parker on Botox at 44, Micro-needling & the Skincare That Works

Nina Parker knows pop culture. The Emmy-nominated television host, podcaster, fashion designer, and reality television host has led pop culture coverage for the past two decades. Nina has built her journalism career on E!, TMZ, VH1, CBS, and now Crooked Media’s Keep It. Her work has given us a front-row seat to the biggest moments and full access to Hollywood’s biggest names. Whether she’s interviewing A-listers on the Met Gala’s red carpet or mediating disagreements on Love & Hip-Hop, Nina brings her expertise and signature style to every moment. But before she commanded screens across multiple television and podcast shows, she learned what it meant to be powerful in Sacramento, California. Nina shared how her parents taught her to prioritize her brilliance by encouraging her to pursue higher education and enrolling her in competitive public speaking.

Nina learned her strengths and how to use her voice against misogyny in the newsrooms where she eventually worked. She shared which beauty and pop culture icons sparked her interest in the entertainment industry, and why. Nina’s relationship with beauty wasn’t as straightforward as her building her personal power. Nina was open about how she used her power to push back against misogyny at TMZ and, inadvertently, impress her newsroom bosses. title: Your Horoscope This Week: October 25 To 31
text:
Your Horoscope This Week: October 25 To 31

Cosmic beings, the final week of October is astrologically charged, with our first full week of Scorpio Season unfolding alongside our first full week of Venus retrograde in Libra. That combination of water and air asks us to honor the intensity of what we feel while also recognizing what is no longer ours to keep carrying. Relationships, financial stress, beauty, self-esteem, and the way we measure our own worth can all come under review. Scorpio wants emotional truth, while Libra wants balance, so this week may reveal where holding on has become heavier than simply letting go. 

On October 26th, the Taurus Full Moon brings some much-needed earth energy into the mix and turns our attention toward the practical ways our lives need to change. Taurus is fixed energy, so there may be something we already know we have outgrown but still feel reluctant to release because it is familiar, comfortable, or once made us feel secure. This Full Moon can make that evolution impossible to ignore. And because it is ruled by Venus retrograde in Libra, the release does not have to be dramatic. There is something powerful about peaceful detachment here: accepting that something had value in one chapter of your life without forcing it to remain valuable forever. 

The second half of the week is about coming down from the Full Moon and simplifying. As the Taurus Moon begins to wane, spend less energy chasing answers and more time grounding yourself in what is already tangible: your body, your environment, the people who consistently show up, and the small pleasures that make life feel full. We end October being asked to define value beyond a number in a bank account or someone else’s approval. What feels stable? What feels nourishing? What is actually worth your energy now? Those answers can tell you a lot about what you are ready to carry into November. 

Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Aries Sun & Rising:

Aries, this first full week of Scorpio Season may feel like shedding a skin you didn’t  realize had become too tight. This is one of the more profound seasons of the year for you because it pulls your attention toward emotional, spiritual, and psychological transformation rather than outward momentum. You may feel more private, more intense, or more aware of the parts of yourself that are ready to evolve. Let the retrogrades slow the process down. You don’t need to force clarity or rush into the  “new you” before you have fully released the version of yourself you’re outgrowing. Some transformations work best when they are allowed to be messy, quiet, and deeply honest. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your money, security, and self worth sector. This could bring a financial windfall, an unexpected expense, or simply a sobering realization about the way you relate to money and stability. Whatever comes up, Taurus energy prefers a steady game plan over an impulsive reaction, especially with Venus retrograde right now. Review what’s working, release what’s draining you,  and get honest about what you actually need in order to feel secure both financially and emotionally. The end of October wants you grounded in what’s real, not rushing toward what is next. 

Taurus Sun & Rising:

Taurus, this first full week of Scorpio Season may make relationships feel a lot more  consuming than usual. You could find yourself excavating every layer of a connection,  reading more deeply into someone’s behavior, or feeling more possessive, protective, or even slightly obsessive about where you stand with people who matter to you. Scorpio energy can make intimacy feel all-or-nothing, and because it sits opposite your sign, it may pull you out of your usual comfort zone by asking you to confront the emotional undercurrents you would normally rather stabilize than dissect. Let yourself notice what is being revealed without turning every feeling into a final conclusion. 

Then your annual Taurus Full Moon arrives on October 26th and brings the focus decisively back to you. A milestone from the past six months may become clear, or you may reach an emotional breaking point that ends up being the breakthrough you needed. This lunation asks you to come back to your body, your needs, your pace, and your own sense of self — the relationship that ultimately sets the tone for every other one. Let yourself feel whatever comes up without immediately trying to move past it, then use that clarity to create a steadier inner and outer foundation so you can end October feeling more rooted in who you are.

Gemini Sun & Rising:

Gemini, this first full week of Scorpio Season asks you to go deeper than the surface level version of wellness. Green smoothies, strength training, and a perfectly organized routine can only take you so far if your mind is exhausted or your inner dialogue is constantly tearing you down. Scorpio energy pushes you to look more honestly at the psychological habits underneath your daily life: the way you speak to yourself, the stress you normalize, and the parts of you that are still performing “fine” when something clearly needs attention. This is a powerful week to shed habits and mindsets that no longer match the person you are becoming, and to replace self criticism with a much more compassionate form of discipline. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lands in your spirituality, solitude, and subconscious sector, which may pull you slightly out of your comfort zone. You’re usually happiest when there’s movement, conversation, and something new to think about, but this lunation asks you to slow down enough to face what has been lingering underneath the noise. Old memories, insecurities, or people from the past may resurface, and the release could be surprisingly physical or emotional. Turn your notifications off, spend more time alone, meditate, journal, sit under a tree, hug one if you feel like it… anything that helps you come back into your body and out of mental overdrive. If you give yourself that space, you could end October feeling dramatically lighter and much more ready to soar into November. 

Cancer Sun & Rising:

Cancer, this first full week of Scorpio Season can feel like your heart is turning the volume up on everything that makes you feel alive. Romance, creativity, pleasure, and inner-child healing all come into sharper focus, but Scorpio asks you to go beyond surface-level fun and notice where desire is tangled up with fear, control, or old emotional conditioning. You may feel more passionate, more magnetic, or more creatively obsessed, but also more aware of what still makes you hesitate to fully enjoy yourself. Let this week show you where joy has been carrying emotional baggage, and give yourself permission to want what you want without immediately interrogating it. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your friendship, community, and future-goals sector, helping you see which people and plans actually feel stable enough to grow with you. A friendship, collaboration, or long-term goal may reach a milestone, or you may realize that a certain social dynamic has run its course. Taurus energy helps you come back to what’s consistent and trustworthy rather than what’s simply exciting in the moment. By the end of the month, you may feel much clearer about who belongs in your next chapter and which dreams are worth building slowly.

Leo Sun & Rising:

Leo, this first full week of Scorpio Season turns your attention toward home, family,  and the emotional foundation underneath everything else. You may feel more protective  of your space, more sensitive to old family dynamics, or more aware of where you have been carrying tension privately while still showing up confidently in public. Scorpio energy can excavate memories, loyalties, and emotional patterns that shaped you long before you had language for them. The goal this week isn’t to fix your entire past; it’s to understand what still has influence over you and decide what deserves to come with you into your next chapter. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your career, reputation, and public-image sector, bringing a culmination around something you’ve been building over the past six months. Recognition, a professional milestone, a decision about your direction, or even a realization that a certain version of success no longer satisfies you could come to the surface. Taurus asks you to move from pressure into sustainability, so pay attention to what feels solid rather than what simply looks impressive. By month’s end, the balance between your private life and public ambitions may feel much clearer, and that clarity can help you build a version of success that actually feels good to live inside of. 

Virgo Sun & Rising:

Virgo, this first full week of Scorpio Season asks you to pay much closer attention to the stories running through your mind all day. Your communication, thinking, learning, and immediate environment are activated, but Scorpio wants more than surface-level  observations. You may become aware of a thought pattern you repeat when you feel insecure, a conversation you keep replaying, or a truth you have been editing because saying it plainly felt too vulnerable. This week is powerful for deeper mental cleanup:  questioning assumptions, naming what you actually feel, and shedding ways of thinking that keep you hyper-vigilant rather than genuinely prepared. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your expansion, travel, education, publishing, and belief sector, helping you zoom out after so much inner analysis. A goal you’ve been working toward over the past six months may reach a milestone, or you may feel ready to make a more grounded decision about where you want to go next. Taurus energy encourages you to trust the path that feels steady and sustainable rather than chasing movement for movement’s sake. By the end of the month, you may realize that your perspective has changed enough to make a whole  new future feel possible.

Libra Sun & Rising:

Libra, this first full week of Scorpio Season pulls you into a deeper conversation with money, self-worth, and the kind of security you actually trust. You may become more aware of where you spend to self-soothe, where you undervalue your time, or where your sense of worth still rises and falls depending on someone else’s approval. Scorpio energy wants you to get underneath the number in the bank account and look at the emotional story attached to it. This is a powerful week to shed scarcity habits,  comparison, or financial choices that no longer reflect who you are becoming, especially with Venus retrograde encouraging you to reassess what feels truly valuable. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your intimacy, shared resources, and transformation sector, bringing a deeper relationship or financial matter to a turning point. A debt, agreement, emotional bond, or trust issue may reach some kind of culmination, and the lesson is to stay grounded enough to see what is actually sustainable. Taurus wants clear terms, steadiness, and reciprocity, so this Full Moon may help you recognize where you are overextended or where support is finally becoming available. By the end of October, you may feel much clearer about what you are willing to share, what you need to protect, and what kind of merging actually feels safe. 

Scorpio Sun & Rising:

Scorpio, this first full week of your birthday season can feel like your energy is finally returning to you. After weeks of retrograde reflection, emotional excavation, and questioning what you still want, the sun in your sign gives you permission to take up more space again. You may feel more magnetic, more certain of your instincts, and more willing to move toward the version of your life that feels deeply yours. This is a powerful reset point for identity, confidence, appearance, desire, and personal direction. Let yourself celebrate how much you have already shed. You are entering a  new solar chapter with more self-knowledge than you had a year ago, and that alone  changes the way you move through everything next. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your partnership sector and may reveal who’s actually equipped to soar with you into this next chapter. A relationship, friendship, collaboration, or commitment could reach an important milestone, while another may make it painfully obvious that loyalty has been keeping you attached past the expiration date. Scorpio can be loyal to a fault once someone has earned a place in your heart, but this Full Moon asks whether the connection is still reciprocal, grounded, and capable of growing with you. Let people reveal who they are. The right ones will not require you to shrink your evolution in order to keep them close. 

Sagittarius Sun & Rising:

Sag, this first full week of Scorpio Season may feel quieter than your usual rhythm, but there is a lot happening beneath the surface. Your solitude, subconscious, and healing zone is activated, so you may crave more privacy, more sleep, or simply more distance from people and situations that keep you mentally overstimulated. Scorpio Season can bring old emotions, fears, or unfinished chapters back into awareness, but the point is not to get lost in them. It is to understand what is draining your energy and what you are finally ready to release before your own season begins next month. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your work, wellness, and daily routine sector, helping you turn that inner awareness into something practical. A habit, responsibility, health matter, or work situation may reach a culmination, or you may realize your body has been trying to tell you something for a while. Taurus energy wants consistency over extremes, so resist the urge to overhaul your entire life overnight. One steady change to your schedule, boundaries, or self-care could do more for you than another burst of motivation that disappears by next week. 

Capricorn Sun & Rising:

Capricorn, this first full week of Scorpio Season puts your attention on the people,  communities, and future plans that actually have enough substance to grow with you. You may feel more selective socially, more protective of your long-term vision, or more aware of which friendships inspire you versus which ones leave you depleted. Scorpio Season can deepen your sense of loyalty, but it can also make you question whether certain alliances are rooted in genuine support or simply history. This is a strong week to get serious about the kind of network you want around the life you are building next. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your romance, creativity, pleasure, and inner-child sector, bringing a much more personal kind of culmination. A love story, creative project, passion, or desire may reach an important milestone, and you may suddenly see how much joy you have been postponing in the name of responsibility. Taurus wants something you can actually feel and enjoy, so let this Full Moon reconnect you with what makes life worth all the effort. By the end of October, you may realize that pleasure deserves a permanent place in your plans, not just whatever time is left over. 

Aquarius Sun & Rising:

Aquarius, this first full week of Scorpio Season puts real weight behind your ambitions and the way you want to be known. Your career, reputation, and public image are activated, but Scorpio energy makes this more than a simple productivity push. You may feel more strategic, more selective about what you attach your name to, and more aware of where you have been chasing visibility without enough emotional investment behind it. This is a strong week to deepen your commitment to the work that actually matters to you and to move with intention rather than trying to prove yourself everywhere at once. 

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th pulls you back toward home, family, and your emotional foundation. A living situation, family matter, or private emotional need may reach a turning point, and you could suddenly realize that external success feels very different when your inner world is unsettled. Taurus energy asks you to stabilize from the inside out. Give yourself permission to slow down, protect your space, and define what security looks like beyond achievement. That grounding can help you end  October feeling much more centered about where you are going next.

Pisces Sun & Rising:

A conversation, writing project, sibling dynamic, decision, or piece of news may reach a turning point and give language to something you have been sensing for weeks. Taurus wants clarity that can actually be used, so simplify what feels overly complicated and say what you mean. By the end of October, you may feel  much more grounded in your own voice and clearer about which ideas are worth carrying forward.

title: The Full Hunter’s Moon In Taurus Will Make You Thirsty For Extra Attention
text:
The Full Hunter’s Moon In Taurus Will Make You Thirsty For Extra Attention

On October 26th, right after midnight on the eastern border, the Full Moon in Taurus appears. October’s Hunter’s Moon (also known as the Travel or Falling Leaves Moon) brightly illuminates the sky, revealing all that is hidden. With Samhain and Halloween less than a week after the lunation, this is an especially sensitive time; the veil between the physical and spiritual worlds is thin, offering moments of heightened intuition. The Hunter’s Moon offers a chance to see in the dark as we shed our past and negative habits to work toward a better present and future. 

Traditionally, the Hunter’s Moon is a time when people would forage for food and track their prey to ensure nourishment in the colder months of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. It is the middle of fall, urging us to work harder to provide for those we care about and wish to protect. This year, the Hunter’s Moon is in the sign of Taurus, exalting the lunar demand for security and indulgence. Not only do we want to build a strong foundation, but we also to have our cake and eat it, too. Nothing is too good for us, and we demand the best of the best. Why not? We deserve it!

The intensity of Pluto in Aquarius, forming a T-square with the sun in Scorpio and the moon in Taurus, isn’t lost on us. The infamous Scorpio stingers may come out as a defense to safeguard our hearts. Hope for transformation and group growth exists if we are willing to access the higher vibration of these planets. However, most of us may not be able to be as levelheaded. When we feel as though others are attacking us right now, we may react fiercely and provocatively, striking back and asserting our feelings. The Scorpion’s poisonous appendages may come out, causing us to use our words to hurt others. As much as we deflect our pain, it won’t help, except for momentary vindication, which is why it’s best to try to mend offenses and build a better dynamic instead.

Luckily, the moon in Taurus aims to give us a softer edge and a calmer approach, and to help us understand that the people in our lives are loyal; conversely, the caveat is that our stubbornness may cause us to dig our heels in the mud when we are pushed to the limit; we are going to scuffle and hustle. Still, the quarrel will be cathartic in the end; the Full Moon in Taurus doesn’t want to end relationships, but enhance them. Keep that in mind before saying things we may regret. Do not take the drama to the extreme.

At this juncture, Venus (the planetary ruler of Taurus, the sign of the Full Moon) is retrograde in Libra (Venus backed up into the air sign on October 25th). Venus retrograde in Libra offers a combustible window of passion — our patience will be tested. The incessant need to partner with others puts pressure on both the other person and us. We might overlook their flaws to keep a commitment going, even though we criticize their behavior. Being kind and compassionate to our partners is essential if forging a relationship is on the horizon. We may also be thirsty for extra attention. There is nothing wrong with requiring affection.

Simultaneously, Mercury is moonwalking in Scorpio (the backslide officially began on October 24th). Revelations from the past will surface as the skeletons we buried deep in our consciousness come out. The reason is that Mercury retrograde in Scorpio is seeking to uncover the truth, and combined with the Full Moon, it offers an opportunity for us to tell those we are close to about our misfortune, insecurities, and emotional states, as we purge ourselves of what we felt was taboo in an effort to be understood. 

Letting go of our old beliefs and invigorating our auras with newness isn’t something that comes easily. But we can shape and tend to who we are and what we value — and seek refuge in the tender arms of a friend, family member, or partner who supports us in these trying times.
